Only 7% of 180 surveyed public LLMs can reliably perform addition without external tools.
The algorithmic implementation is consistent across seeds and model sizes, with attention heads and MLPs satisfying strict constraints.
papers.limitation:
The analysis does not examine the specific data representations and transformations used by polysemantic nodes, SGN nodes, and OPR nodes in the residual stream, nor the detailed mechanisms of MLP layers.
The automated framework for discovering algorithm subtasks has limitations and some aspects are specific to the math models studied.
Fully reverse engineering neural networks is challenging due to distributed parallel computations difficult to trace to specific components.
future_direction: Refine the declarative language for describing algorithms and the framework for testing these descriptions against models.
Further work to understand how identified components actually encode and manipulate information.
Investigate the universality of representations and circuits across models using the provided models.
papers.abstract: Transformers are widely deployed in large language models (LLMs), yet most models still fail on basic arithmetic tasks such as multidigit addition. In contrast, we show that small transformers trained from scratch can solve n-digit addition and subtraction with 99.999% accuracy. Building directly on prior work that uncovered addition circuits, we extend the analysis to subtraction and present a unified mechanistic account based on cascading carry and borrow circuits. Using a suite of 49 trained models, we apply systematic ablations and node-level constraints to validate the learned mechanisms and release a reproducible interpretability toolkit for studying arithmetic circuits. Finally, surveying 180 publicly available LLMs, we find that only 7% can reliably perform addition, underscoring the gap between specialized small models and general-purpose LLMs. Our results show that arithmetic can be implemented exactly by tiny transformers, offering a tractable case study for mechanistic interpretability and a cautionary contrast with the persistent arithmetic failures of much larger models.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: Disentangling Direction and Magnitude in Transformer Representations: A Double Dissociation Through L2-Matched Perturbation Analysis
papers.research_question: What are the distinct functional roles of direction (orientation) and magnitude (norm) in transformer hidden state representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces L2-matched perturbation analysis to discover a double dissociation: angular perturbations disproportionately damage language modeling loss, while magnitude perturbations disproportionately damage syntactic accuracy, with distinct mechanistic pathways through attention and LayerNorm.
papers.conclusion: Direction and magnitude serve partially distinct computational roles in LayerNorm-based transformers: direction preferentially governs attentional routing, while magnitude encodes structural position and modulates processing intensity through LayerNorm.
papers.key_findings:
Angular perturbations cause up to 42.9× more damage to language modeling loss than magnitude perturbations at equal Euclidean displacement.
Magnitude perturbations cause up to 20.4% greater drop in syntactic accuracy (subject-verb agreement) than angular perturbations.
Causal intervention shows angular damage is substantially mediated by attention pathways (28.4% recovery via repair), while magnitude damage is substantially mediated by LayerNorm pathways (29.9% recovery).
The dissociation pattern replicates across scales within the Pythia architecture family but reverses in RMSNorm-based architectures like TinyLlama.
Magnitude correlates with parse tree depth, and disrupting this correlation explains why magnitude perturbations specifically impair syntactic processing.
papers.limitation:
L2 matching assumes equal Euclidean distance makes perturbations comparable, but neural networks operate in anisotropic spaces; angular perturbations amplify 3× more than magnitude by the final layer.
Angular perturbations use random orthogonal directions; results might differ for systematic rotations toward known feature directions.
Findings are specific to the Pythia/OPT architecture family and do not generalize to all transformers; the pattern reverses in RMSNorm-based architectures (TinyLlama).
Only middle layers (8–15) were targeted for intervention; early and late layers may show different patterns.
Syntactic evaluation is limited to subject-verb agreement from BLiMP; other syntactic phenomena may show different patterns.
Causal repair experiments account for only ~30% of each perturbation's damage; the remaining ~70% likely flows through MLP layers and residual connections.
future_direction: Feature-specific rotations (systematic rotations toward/away from known feature directions).
Investigating how the roles of direction and magnitude evolve during training.
Exploring magnitude as a confidence signal for uncertainty quantification.
Extending the methodology to other modalities (e.g., vision transformers).
Systematic comparison across normalization schemes (LayerNorm vs. RMSNorm).
papers.abstract: Transformer hidden states encode information as high-dimensional vectors, yet whether direction (orientation in representational space) and magnitude (vector norm) serve distinct functional roles remains unclear. Studying Pythia-family models, we discover a striking cross-over dissociation: angular perturbations cause up to 42.9 more damage to language modeling loss, while magnitude perturbations cause disproportionately more damage to syntactic processing (20.4% vs.1.6% accuracy drop on subject-verb agreement).This finding is enabled by L2-matched perturbation analysis, a methodology ensuring that an gular and magnitude perturbations achieve identical Euclidean displacements. Causal intervention reveals that angular damage flows substantially through the attention pathways (28.4% loss recovery via attention repair), while magnitude damage flows partly through the LayerNorm pathways(29.9% recovery via LayerNorm repair). These patterns replicate across scales within the Pythia architecture family. These findings provide evidence that direction and magnitude support partially distinct computational roles in LayerNorm based architectures. The direction preferentially affects attentional routing, while magnitude modulates processing intensity for fine-grained syntactic judgments. We find different patterns in RMSNorm-based architectures, suggesting that the dissociation depends on architectural choices. Our results refine the linear representation hypothesis and have implications for model editing and interpretability research

papers.title: Circuit Component Reuse Across Tasks in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and whether insights from circuit analysis generalize across tasks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and that interventions based on one circuit can improve performance on another task, providing evidence for task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.conclusion: Circuit components are reused across tasks, providing evidence that large language models' behavior can be explained in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.key_findings:
The IOI circuit reproduces on GPT2-Medium, with minor differences such as the negative mover head attending only to the S2 token.
The Colored Objects circuit shares about 78% of the important attention heads with the IOI circuit, indicating high component reuse.
Interventions on inhibition heads and the negative mover head can boost accuracy on the Colored Objects task from 49.6% to 93.7%.
The inhibition-mover head subcircuit behaves invariantly across tasks, as predicted by the IOI circuit.
The negative mover head in GPT2-Medium exhibits more sophisticated behavior than in GPT2-Small, directly demoting the subject token.
papers.limitation:
Quantifying circuit overlap is complex and not fully addressed in this paper.
The generality of the circuit beyond the studied tasks is not confirmed.
future_direction: Understanding how commonly the mover circuit is used by GPT2 in other tasks.
Developing methods for quantifying circuit overlap.
Studying circuit reuse in larger models.
papers.abstract: Recent work in mechanistic interpretability has shown that behaviors in language models can be successfully reverse-engineered through circuit analysis. A common criticism, however, is that each circuit is task-specific, and thus such analysis cannot contribute to understanding the models at a higher level. In this work, we present evidence that insights (both low-level findings about specific heads and higher-level findings about general algorithms) can indeed generalize across tasks. Specifically, we study the circuit discovered in Wang et al. (2022) for the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task and 1.) show that it reproduces on a larger GPT2 model, and 2.) that it is mostly reused to solve a seemingly different task: Colored Objects (Ippolito & Callison-Burch, 2023). We provide evidence that the process underlying both tasks is functionally very similar, and contains about a 78% overlap in in-circuit attention heads. We further present a proof-of-concept intervention experiment, in which we adjust four attention heads in middle layers in order to 'repair' the Colored Objects circuit and make it behave like the IOI circuit. In doing so, we boost accuracy from 49.6% to 93.7% on the Colored Objects task and explain most sources of error. The intervention affects downstream attention heads in specific ways predicted by their interactions in the IOI circuit, indicating that this subcircuit behavior is invariant to the different task inputs. Overall, our results provide evidence that it may yet be possible to explain large language models' behavior in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks and computational components.

papers.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
papers.research_question: Do circuit analyses of LLMs generalize across training time and model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Circuit analyses are consistent across training and scale: task abilities and supporting functional components emerge at similar token counts across model sizes, and the overarching algorithms implemented by circuits remain stable even when individual components change.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analyses generalize well over both training and scale, suggesting that studies on small models at the end of pre-training can inform understanding of larger models and models with longer training.
papers.key_findings:
Task abilities and functional components (e.g., induction heads, name-mover heads) emerge consistently at similar token counts across different model scales.
The algorithm implemented by a circuit remains stable over training even when the specific attention heads implementing it change.
Circuit size correlates with model size and can fluctuate over time while the algorithm remains the same.
Components like induction heads emerge around 2B tokens across scales, paralleling task learning curves.
Circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training provide insights that generalize to larger models and longer training runs.
papers.limitation:
The study does not include fine-tuning or other post-training techniques.
Circuit completeness is challenging to verify.
The findings need validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
future_direction: Validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
Investigating the load-balancing mechanism that maintains task performance when components change.
papers.abstract: Most currently deployed large language models (LLMs) undergo continuous training or additional finetuning. By contrast, most research into LLMs' internal mechanisms focuses on models at one snapshot in time (the end of pre-training), raising the question of whether their results generalize to real-world settings. Existing studies of mechanisms over time focus on encoder-only or toy models, which differ significantly from most deployed models. In this study, we track how model mechanisms, operationalized as circuits, emerge and evolve across 300 billion tokens of training in decoder-only LLMs, in models ranging from 70 million to 2.8 billion parameters. We find that task abilities and the functional components that support them emerge consistently at similar token counts across scale. Moreover, although such components may be implemented by different attention heads over time, the overarching algorithm that they implement remains. Surprisingly, both these algorithms and the types of components involved therein can replicate across model scale. These results suggest that circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training can provide insights that still apply after additional pre-training and over model scale.

papers.title: Understanding Counting Mechanisms in Large Language and Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models (LLMs) and large vision-language models (LVLMs) represent and compute numerical information in counting tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces CountScope, a tool for mechanistic interpretability of counting, and identifies an internal counter mechanism in LLMs and LVLMs that updates with each item and is stored in the final token or visual region.
papers.conclusion: Counting emerges as a structured, layerwise process in LLMs and follows the same general pattern in LVLMs, shaped by the properties of the vision encoder.
papers.key_findings:
Individual tokens or visual features encode latent positional count information that can be extracted and transferred across contexts.
Layerwise analyses reveal a progressive emergence of numerical representations, with lower layers encoding small counts and higher layers representing larger ones.
An internal counter mechanism updates with each item, stored mainly in the final token or region and transferable between contexts.
In LVLMs, numerical information also appears in visual embeddings, shifting between background and foreground regions depending on spatial composition.
Models rely on structural cues such as separators in text, which act as shortcuts for tracking item counts and influence the accuracy of numerical predictions.
papers.abstract: This paper examines how large language models (LLMs) and large vision-language models (LVLMs) represent and compute numerical information in counting tasks. We use controlled experiments with repeated textual and visual items and analyze model behavior through causal mediation and activation patching. To this end, we design a specialized tool, CountScope, for mechanistic interpretability of numerical content. Results show that individual tokens or visual features encode latent positional count information that can be extracted and transferred across contexts. Layerwise analyses reveal a progressive emergence of numerical representations, with lower layers encoding small counts and higher layers representing larger ones. We identify an internal counter mechanism that updates with each item, stored mainly in the final token or region and transferable between contexts. In LVLMs, numerical information also appears in visual embeddings, shifting between background and foreground regions depending on spatial composition. Models rely on structural cues such as separators in text, which act as shortcuts for tracking item counts and influence the accuracy of numerical predictions. Overall, counting emerges as a structured, layerwise process in LLMs and follows the same general pattern in LVLMs, shaped by the properties of the vision encoder.

papers.title: Signal in the Noise: Polysemantic Interference Transfers and Predicts Cross-Model Influence
papers.research_question: How can polysemantic interference structures in language models be exploited to manipulate model outputs, and do these interference patterns transfer across models of different scales and families?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that polysemantic interference structures in language models create a systematic vulnerability, and that interventions based on these structures, identified in small models, can transfer to larger instruction-tuned models for predictable behavioral control without requiring access to their internals.
papers.conclusion: Polysemantic interference reveals a systematic vulnerability in language models, and the generalization of these structures across scale and family challenges the view of polysemanticity as purely stochastic, offering new avenues for black-box control and theoretical insight into internal representation.
papers.key_findings:
Interventions leveraging polysemantic structures (feature-direction steering, token-gradient steering, prompt injection) can effectively manipulate model next-token predictions.
Polysemantic interference patterns are persistent across models: interventions distilled from small models (Pythia-70M, GPT-2-Small) transfer reliably to larger models (Llama-3.1, Gemma-2).
Many counterintuitive interference patterns are stable across models but remain largely opaque to human interpretation, suggesting models learn robust regularities not aligned with surface semantics.
Highly polysemantic neurons are more vulnerable to interventions; amplifying 'super-neurons' (activated by many features) strongly alters model behavior, while deactivating them has a reduced effect.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on sparse autoencoders (SAEs) whose outputs fluctuate with dimensionality and hyperparameters, yielding unstable features.
Interventions steer only one interference feature in one layer, while multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations could amplify and better obscure the effect.
Vulnerability is quantified solely via shifts in immediate next-token probabilities on two small base models, with only coarse transfer checks on larger instructed models.
future_direction: Establishing how these interventions alter non-trivial downstream tasks in bigger models.
Exploring multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations to amplify and better obscure intervention effects.
papers.abstract: Polysemanticity is pervasive in language models and remains a major challenge for interpretation and model behavioral control. Leveraging sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we map the polysemantic topology of two small models (Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small) to identify SAE feature pairs that are semantically unrelated yet exhibit interference within models. We intervene at four loci (prompt, token, feature, neuron) and measure induced shifts in the next-token prediction distribution, uncovering polysemantic structures that expose a systematic vulnerability in these models. Critically, interventions distilled from counterintuitive interference patterns shared by two small models transfer reliably to larger instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct), yielding predictable behavioral shifts without access to model internals. These findings challenge the view that polysemanticity is purely stochastic, demonstrating instead that interference structures generalize across scale and family. Such generalization suggests a convergent, higher-order organization of internal representations, which is only weakly aligned with intuition and structured by latent regularities, offering new possibilities for both black-box control and theoretical insight into human and artificial cognition.

papers.title: Emergent effects of scaling on the functional hierarchies within large language models
papers.research_question: What is the functional hierarchy of abstraction across layers in LLMs, and how does it change with model scaling?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models exhibit functional hierarchies with abstraction increasing across layers, but scaling introduces deviations such as double representation peaks and anti-persistent fluctuations in attention mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The study confirms functional hierarchies in LLMs but reveals emergent deviations with scaling, such as double representation peaks and layer coordination, complicating interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Item-level semantics are most strongly represented in early layers (2-7), two-item relations in middle layers (8-12), and four-item analogies in later layers (10-15), consistent with an abstraction hierarchy.
Deep layers can represent narrow two-item relations from early in the context, suggesting information compression without meaningful abstraction.
In the large Llama-3.3-70b-Instruct model, representation of two-item relations and analogies shows two distinct peaks (layers 12-16 and 25-33), indicating fluctuations in abstraction level.
Adjacent layers in the large model exhibit anti-persistent fluctuations in attention outputs, with negative autocorrelation, suggesting coordinated specialization.
Buried concepts (target text followed by filler) are represented in deeper layers, showing that late layers capture global document-wide information.
papers.limitation:
The interpretation of the double-peak pattern and valley in large models is unclear and requires further work.
Analyses on grammar and syntax were inconclusive and not reported, limiting insights into syntactic processing.
future_direction: Study larger models to understand scaling effects further.
Investigate the mechanisms behind the double-peak representation and layer coordination.
Explore how late-layer representations can be used for steering and safety applications.
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) architectures are often described as functionally hierarchical: Early layers process syntax, middle layers begin to parse semantics, and late layers integrate information. The present work revisits these ideas. This research submits simple texts to an LLM (e.g., "A church and organ") and extracts the resulting activations. Then, for each layer, support vector machines and ridge regressions are fit to predict a text's label and thus examine whether a given layer encodes some information. Analyses using a small model (Llama-3.2-3b; 28 layers) partly bolster the common hierarchical perspective: Item-level semantics are most strongly represented early (layers 2-7), then two-item relations (layers 8-12), and then four-item analogies (layers 10-15). Afterward, the representation of items and simple relations gradually decreases in deeper layers that focus on more global information. However, several findings run counter to a steady hierarchy view: First, although deep layers can represent document-wide abstractions, deep layers also compress information from early portions of the context window without meaningful abstraction. Second, when examining a larger model (Llama-3.3-70b-Instruct), stark fluctuations in abstraction level appear: As depth increases, two-item relations and four-item analogies initially increase in their representation, then markedly decrease, and afterward increase again momentarily. This peculiar pattern consistently emerges across several experiments. Third, another emergent effect of scaling is coordination between the attention mechanisms of adjacent layers. Across multiple experiments using the larger model, adjacent layers fluctuate between what information they each specialize in representing. In sum, an abstraction hierarchy often manifests across layers, but large models also deviate from this structure in curious ways.

papers.title: Uncovering Emergent Physics Representations Learned In-Context by Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models implicitly learn physics during in-context learning, and do recognizable physical quantities emerge as distinct features in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that large language models can learn to forecast physical dynamics via in-context learning, and that energy-related features emerge in their residual stream activations, which are causally important for accurate predictions.
papers.conclusion: The results demonstrate that LLMs can internalize physical concepts like energy during in-context learning, suggesting transformer architectures can internalize abstract reasoning priors similar to human abstraction.
papers.key_findings:
Prediction accuracy for physical dynamics forecasting improves with longer context length.
Sparse activations from sparse autoencoders (SAEs) applied to residual streams correlate with energy quantities (total, kinetic, potential).
The correlation between sparse activations and energy is context-dependent and increases with longer contexts, especially for chaotic systems.
Intervention experiments ablating energy-correlated sparse activations degrade prediction accuracy, indicating their functional role.
Energy-related features are most prominently captured in the middle layers of the transformer.
papers.limitation: The study uses raw trajectory values as the sole input modality without external instructions or prompting strategies, leaving open whether chain-of-thought or structured prompts would strengthen correlations.
future_direction: Explore physics concepts beyond classical mechanics.
Investigate more human-aligned tasks such as answering conceptual questions from physics exams.
Leverage physics-informed tasks to understand internal mechanisms of large-scale models and advance LLM-based agents for physically realistic environments.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive in-context learning (ICL) abilities, enabling them to solve wide range of tasks via textual prompts alone. As these capabilities advance, the range of applicable domains continues to expand significantly. However, identifying the precise mechanisms or internal structures within LLMs that allow successful ICL across diverse, distinct classes of tasks remains elusive. Physics-based tasks offer a promising testbed for probing this challenge. Unlike synthetic sequences such as basic arithmetic or symbolic equations, physical systems provide experimentally controllable, real-world data based on structured dynamics grounded in fundamental principles. This makes them particularly suitable for studying the emergent reasoning behaviors of LLMs in a realistic yet tractable setting. Here, we mechanistically investigate the ICL ability of LLMs, especially focusing on their ability to reason about physics. Using a dynamics forecasting task in physical systems as a proxy, we evaluate whether LLMs can learn physics in context. We first show that the performance of dynamics forecasting in context improves with longer input contexts. To uncover how such capability emerges in LLMs, we analyze the model's residual stream activations using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). Our experiments reveal that the features captured by SAEs correlate with key physical variables, such as energy. These findings demonstrate that meaningful physical concepts are encoded within LLMs during in-context learning. In sum, our work provides a novel case study that broadens our understanding of how LLMs learn in context.

papers.title: Superposition Yields Robust Neural Scaling
papers.research_question: How does superposition influence the loss scaling with model dimension, and under what conditions does loss follow a power law with what exponent?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that representation superposition leads to robust inverse scaling of loss with model dimension, and that real LLMs operate in the strong superposition regime, explaining neural scaling laws.
papers.conclusion: Superposition is a central driver of neural scaling laws, providing insights into when scaling laws hold and when they break down.
papers.key_findings:
In the weak superposition regime, loss scales as a power law only if feature frequencies follow a power law, with exponent α-1.
In the strong superposition regime, loss scales inversely with model dimension (1/m) due to geometric overlaps, robust across a broad class of feature frequency distributions.
Real LLMs (Opt, GPT2, Qwen, Pythia) operate in the strong superposition regime and exhibit loss scaling inversely with model dimension, consistent with the toy model predictions.
Weight decay can be used to control the degree of superposition in the toy model, enabling systematic study of scaling behaviors.
The Chinchilla scaling laws are consistent with the strong superposition regime, with loss scaling inversely with model dimension.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is based on a toy model and observations without rigorously solving the toy model, limiting deeper theoretical understanding.
The underlying reasons why LLMs operate in the strong superposition regime were not studied in detail.
The study does not address scaling laws with dataset size and training steps.
future_direction: Study the effect of softmax and other non-linearities, as well as the role of sparsity in language.
More theoretical studies on scaling laws inspired by this work.
Study scaling laws with dataset size and training steps.
papers.abstract: The success of today's large language models (LLMs) depends on the observation that larger models perform better. However, the origin of this neural scaling law, that loss decreases as a power law with model size, remains unclear. We propose that representation superposition, meaning that LLMs represent more features than they have dimensions, can be a key contributor to loss and cause neural scaling. Based on Anthropic's toy model, we use weight decay to control the degree of superposition, allowing us to systematically study how loss scales with model size. When superposition is weak, the loss follows a power law only if data feature frequencies are power-law distributed. In contrast, under strong superposition, the loss generically scales inversely with model dimension across a broad class of frequency distributions, due to geometric overlaps between representation vectors. We confirmed that open-sourced LLMs operate in the strong superposition regime and have loss scaling inversely with model dimension, and that the Chinchilla scaling laws are also consistent with this behavior. Our results identify representation superposition as a central driver of neural scaling laws, providing insights into questions like when neural scaling laws can be improved and when they will break down.

papers.title: Language Models Understand Us, Poorly
papers.research_question: What does it mean for language models to understand human language, and can current and future models achieve such understanding?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that understanding-as-representation is a necessary view for advancing a science of understanding, and that current models lack the necessary data and inductive biases to achieve human-like understanding, with scaling alone being insufficient.
papers.conclusion: Present language models have limited access to meaning, and scale alone may not be sufficient to achieve human-level understanding until we can guarantee similar representations or inductive biases.
papers.key_findings:
Current language and multi-modal models are pragmatically challenged by under-specification of form, meaning they lack data on aspects of language like dynamics, intersubjectivity, and grounding.
The Scaling Paradigm, which assumes scale alone (more parameters, data, modalities) will lead to human-like understanding, may be computationally infeasible and insufficient.
Understanding-as-representation, which focuses on internal, dynamical representations, is a more fruitful approach than understanding-as-mapping or understanding-as-reliability for advancing a science of understanding.
Present language models have limited access to meaning and do not understand in the same way humans do; attributing full understanding to them is premature.
Future work should probe model internals, add more of human language (e.g., intersubjective, multi-agent environments), and measure what models can learn to bridge the gap.
papers.limitation:
This is only one perspective of many possible on the nature of understanding.
Given the short form of this presentation I am not able to do justice to the diverse fields–from philosophy of science to linguistics to brain science–which I reference.
I may therefore insufficiently explain the relevant literature to my target readers in NLP.
While I have attempted to present a well-informed prior on the future direction of AI, my perspective is nonetheless uncertain; I may ultimately be incorrect.
future_direction: Probe model internals through functional analysis and causal interventions.
Add more of human language such as intersubjective, multi-agent environments, dynamic grounding, and common sense.
Measure what models can learn, including the tractability of meaning and the scaling factors required as more aspects of human language are included.
papers.abstract: Some claim language models understand us. Others won't hear it. To clarify, I investigate three views of human language understanding: as-mapping, as-reliability and as-representation. I argue that while behavioral reliability is necessary for understanding, internal representations are sufficient; they climb the right hill. I review state-of-the-art language and multi-modal models: they are pragmatically challenged by under-specification of form. I question the Scaling Paradigm: limits on resources may prohibit scaled-up models from approaching understanding. Last, I describe how as-representation advances a science of understanding. We need work which probes model internals, adds more of human language, and measures what models can learn.

papers.title: Positional Description Matters for Transformers Arithmetic
papers.research_question: How does positional encoding affect transformers' performance on arithmetic tasks, and how can we modify positional encoding or data representation to improve performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers' poor arithmetic performance stems from over-reliance on positional information, and proposes methods like padding, reversing products, and random embedding to improve performance, enabling small models to achieve high accuracy on large-digit multiplication and addition.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that with appropriate modifications to positional encoding or data format, small transformers can perform complex arithmetic tasks, highlighting the importance of positional information in arithmetic reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Padding and reversing the product order enable a small transformer to perform 15-digit multiplication with high accuracy.
Using random spaces or recursive scratchpad formats improves length generalization in addition tasks.
Random embedding (a novel positional encoding) improves generalization for both digit reversion and addition tasks.
Integrating arithmetic data with natural language dialogue is challenging but can be improved by removing absolute positional embedding or using random embedding.
Including simple cases (like n×1 multiplication) in training helps models learn complex multiplication.
papers.limitation:
The experiments did not fine-tune hyperparameters, so higher accuracy for more digits might be possible with larger training sets, better digit distributions, or tuned learning rates.
The approaches for multiplication, length extrapolation, and natural language integration are tackled separately; a single model combining all properties is left for future work.
future_direction: Combining the proposed approaches into a single model that excels at all arithmetic challenges.
Exploring the methods on larger models and more complex arithmetic tasks.
papers.abstract: Transformers, central to the successes in modern Natural Language Processing, often falter on arithmetic tasks despite their vast capabilities --which paradoxically include remarkable coding abilities. We observe that a crucial challenge is their naive reliance on positional information to solve arithmetic problems with a small number of digits, leading to poor performance on larger numbers. Herein, we delve deeper into the role of positional encoding, and propose several ways to fix the issue, either by modifying the positional encoding directly, or by modifying the representation of the arithmetic task to leverage standard positional encoding differently. We investigate the value of these modifications for three tasks: (i) classical multiplication, (ii) length extrapolation in addition, and (iii) addition in natural language context. For (i) we train a small model on a small dataset (100M parameters and 300k samples) with remarkable aptitude in (direct, no scratchpad) 15 digits multiplication and essentially perfect up to 12 digits, while usual training in this context would give a model failing at 4 digits multiplication. In the experiments on addition, we use a mere 120k samples to demonstrate: for (ii) extrapolation from 10 digits to testing on 12 digits numbers while usual training would have no extrapolation, and for (iii) almost perfect accuracy up to 5 digits while usual training would be correct only up to 3 digits (which is essentially memorization with a training set of 120k samples).

papers.title: Does Circuit Analysis Interpretability Scale? Evidence from Multiple Choice Capabilities in Chinchilla
papers.research_question: Does circuit analysis interpretability scale to large language models, specifically for the algorithmic task of multiple-choice question answering?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that existing circuit analysis techniques (logit attribution, attention pattern visualization, activation patching) scale to a 70B parameter model, allowing identification and partial understanding of the circuit for multiple-choice question answering, particularly 'correct letter' heads.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analysis techniques can scale to large models, but the features used to implement algorithmic tasks can be messy in their semantics, even when limited to a distribution with little superposition.
papers.key_findings:
Identified 45 nodes (attention heads and MLPs) that are causally responsible for most of the model's performance on the multiple-choice task.
Categorized attention heads into four types: 'Correct Letter', 'Uniform', 'Single Letter', and 'Amplification'.
Found that 'correct letter' heads attend to the correct answer label and copy it to the output logits.
Used SVD to compress query/key/value subspaces of 'correct letter' heads, finding the query and key subspaces represent an 'Nth item in an enumeration' feature, but this is only a partial explanation for behavior on a more general distribution.
Showed that the algorithmic task of mapping the correct answer to its label is interpretable, but the specific features used are messy and only partially understood.
papers.limitation:
The effect of patching a node can be compensated by downstream nodes (backup behavior), potentially distorting results.
The analysis only finds a cross-section of the circuit (nodes separating ancestors and descendants) rather than the full set of relevant nodes.
Results are only applicable to the specific distribution tested (MMLU subset).
Focused on the net effect on the correct label, neglecting the part of the circuit that identifies the set of possible answer tokens.
future_direction: Investigating the rest of the circuit (nodes feeding into the correct letter heads).
Comparing different approaches to causal interventions (e.g., noising vs. denoising).
Automating circuit analysis to reduce labor intensity.
papers.abstract: \emph{Circuit analysis} is a promising technique for understanding the internal mechanisms of language models. However, existing analyses are done in small models far from the state of the art. To address this, we present a case study of circuit analysis in the 70B Chinchilla model, aiming to test the scalability of circuit analysis. In particular, we study multiple-choice question answering, and investigate Chinchilla's capability to identify the correct answer \emph{label} given knowledge of the correct answer \emph{text}. We find that the existing techniques of logit attribution, attention pattern visualization, and activation patching naturally scale to Chinchilla, allowing us to identify and categorize a small set of `output nodes' (attention heads and MLPs). We further study the `correct letter' category of attention heads aiming to understand the semantics of their features, with mixed results. For normal multiple-choice question answers, we significantly compress the query, key and value subspaces of the head without loss of performance when operating on the answer labels for multiple-choice questions, and we show that the query and key subspaces represent an `Nth item in an enumeration' feature to at least some extent. However, when we attempt to use this explanation to understand the heads' behaviour on a more general distribution including randomized answer labels, we find that it is only a partial explanation, suggesting there is more to learn about the operation of `correct letter' heads on multiple choice question answering.

papers.title: Distilled Circuits: A Mechanistic Study of Internal Restructuring in Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge distillation restructure internal circuits and representations in student models, and how can functional alignment between teacher and student be quantified?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic understanding of how knowledge distillation restructures internal circuits, showing that students compress and discard teacher components, and introduces an alignment metric to quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity.
papers.conclusion: While student models preserve broad functional behavior from their teachers, knowledge distillation causes significant internal circuit restructuring, leading to increased reliance on fewer components and reduced robustness. The alignment metric captures functional similarity beyond output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, leading to stronger reliance on fewer components.
Student models are more vulnerable to component ablation, indicating reduced robustness.
The introduced alignment metric effectively quantifies functional alignment between teacher and student models.
These findings on internal restructuring and reduced robustness generalize across different model architectures (GPT2, BERT, Llama).
Performance similarity does not guarantee similarity in internal computation; circuit-level analysis is essential for understanding functional alignment.
papers.limitation:
The study is constrained by the relatively small set of models evaluated (6).
The component role attribution procedure is manual and could be automated.
The alignment metric could be improved in granularity and interpretability.
The findings are based on specific tasks and models and may not generalize to all settings.
future_direction: Apply the methodology and alignment metric to a broader, more diverse collection of models.
Automate the component role attribution procedure, potentially using interpretability agents.
Improve the alignment metric's granularity and interpretability, and explore incorporating it as a loss term during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses a larger neural model (teacher) into smaller, faster student models by training them to match teacher outputs. However, the internal computational transformations that occur during this process remain poorly understood. We apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to analyze how internal circuits, representations, and activation patterns differ between teacher and student. Focusing on GPT2-small and its distilled counterpart DistilGPT2, we find that student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, often resulting in stronger reliance on fewer individual components. To quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity, we introduce an alignment metric based on influence-weighted component similarity, validated across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: Addition in Four Movements: Mapping Layer-wise Information Trajectories in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct perform multi-digit addition through structured, algorithmic computation (e.g., digit-wise summation with carry propagation), or through non-algorithmic pattern extraction?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a consistent four-stage, layer-wise ordering of information when LLMs perform multi-digit addition (formula structure, core computations, numerical abstractions, output alignment), supporting a hierarchical, computation-first account rather than rote pattern matching.
papers.conclusion: The sequential emergence of features supports a structured, computation-like process in LLMs for addition, rather than rote memorization, and the observed trajectory is robust across architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Early layers (1) encode formula structure (operand/operator layout) while the gold next token is still far from top-1.
Mid layers (2) expose digit-wise sums and carry indicators.
Deeper layers (3) express result-level numerical abstractions that support near-perfect digit decoding from hidden states.
Near the output (4), representations align with final sequence generation, with the correct next token reliably ranked first.
The four-stage ordering is consistent across experiments and models (with minor depth shifts), with each signal family becoming linearly decodable with high accuracy (typically ≥95%).
papers.limitation:
Correlation vs. causation: linear probes and logit lens are correlational, not causal.
Task scope: only in-distribution, base-10 multi-digit addition under short prompts.
Model specificity: main analysis on LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, though other models show similar ordering but with varying layer indices.
future_direction: Causal interventions (e.g., activation patching, targeted ablations) to establish dependence on intermediate computations.
papers.abstract: Multi-digit addition is a clear probe of the computational power of large language models. To dissect the internal arithmetic processes in LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, we combine linear probing with logit-lens inspection. Inspired by the step-by-step manner in which humans perform addition, we propose and analyze a coherent four-stage trajectory in the forward pass:Formula-structure representations become linearly decodable first, while the answer token is still far down the candidate list.Core computational features then emerge prominently.At deeper activation layers, numerical abstractions of the result become clearer, enabling near-perfect detection and decoding of the individual digits in the sum.Near the output, the model organizes and generates the final content, with the correct token reliably occupying the top rank.This trajectory suggests a hierarchical process that favors internal computation over rote memorization. We release our code and data to facilitate reproducibility.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Analysis of a Transformer Trained on a Symbolic Multi-Step Reasoning Task
papers.research_question: How does a transformer internally solve a symbolic multi-step reasoning task, specifically pathfinding in trees? What interpretable mechanisms does it use?
papers.core_contribution: The transformer implements an interpretable backward chaining algorithm for pathfinding, using deduction heads to climb the tree, parallel computation via register tokens, and a one-step lookahead heuristic.
papers.conclusion: The transformer demonstrates deductive reasoning up to a depth bounded by its layers, using parallelized backward chaining and heuristics, suggesting an inductive bias towards parallelized strategies for reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The first layer attention head performs edge token concatenation, copying source node information to target node positions.
Deduction heads in subsequent layers implement backward chaining, climbing the tree one level per layer.
For paths longer than the number of layers, the model uses register tokens to perform parallel backward chaining and merges subpaths.
The model employs a one-step lookahead heuristic that identifies child nodes and increases logits for non-leaf children.
The model's reasoning depth is bounded by the number of layers, beyond which it resorts to heuristics.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is on a synthetic symbolic task, and it is unclear if similar mechanisms exist in large language models trained on natural language.
The analysis is limited to input where the edge list is presented in backward order; other arrangements may lead to different mechanisms.

papers.title: The Clock and the Pizza: Two Stories in Mechanistic Explanation of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Do neural networks, trained on well-understood algorithmic tasks, reliably re-discover known algorithms for solving those tasks, and under what conditions do they discover familiar algorithmic solutions?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on modular addition can discover qualitatively different algorithms (Clock, Pizza, and others), with the algorithm learned depending on hyperparameters like attention rate and width, revealing algorithmic phase transitions and the need for tools to characterize algorithmic phase spaces.
papers.conclusion: Algorithmic discoveries in neural networks are not inevitable; even simple tasks admit a diversity of solutions, motivating the development of tools to characterize the algorithmic phase space of neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Networks can learn either the previously described Clock algorithm or a new, less intuitive Pizza algorithm for modular addition.
The Pizza algorithm uses averaging and absolute value operations, while the Clock algorithm uses multiplication via attention.
Models sometimes implement multiple, parallel copies of an algorithm (ensembling) for robustness.
Sharp algorithmic phase transitions between Clock and Pizza occur as model hyperparameters (attention rate, width) are varied.
Non-circular algorithms also exist, especially in deeper networks or with low attention rates.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on a single learning problem (modular addition), and scaling the techniques to more complex models and real-world tasks requires significant additional work.
future_direction: How to find, classify, and interpret unfamiliar algorithms in a systematic way.
How to disentangle multiple, parallel algorithm implementations in the presence of ensembling.
papers.abstract: Do neural networks, trained on well-understood algorithmic tasks, reliably rediscover known algorithms for solving those tasks? Several recent studies, on tasks ranging from group arithmetic to in-context linear regression, have suggested that the answer is yes. Using modular addition as a prototypical problem, we show that algorithm discovery in neural networks is sometimes more complex. Small changes to model hyperparameters and initializations can induce the discovery of qualitatively different algorithms from a fixed training set, and even parallel implementations of multiple such algorithms. Some networks trained to perform modular addition implement a familiar Clock algorithm; others implement a previously undescribed, less intuitive, but comprehensible procedure which we term the Pizza algorithm, or a variety of even more complex procedures. Our results show that even simple learning problems can admit a surprising diversity of solutions, motivating the development of new tools for characterizing the behavior of neural networks across their algorithmic phase space.

papers.title: Emergent World Representations: Exploring a Sequence Model Trained on a Synthetic Task
papers.research_question: Does a sequence model trained on a synthetic task (Othello game transcripts) learn an internal representation of the board state, and is that representation causal to its predictions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that a GPT model trained on Othello game transcripts learns a nonlinear internal representation of the board state, which is causally involved in its predictions. It introduces intervention techniques and latent saliency maps for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The experiments provide evidence that Othello-GPT maintains a nonlinear internal representation of the game board state, which is causally linked to its predictions. The tools introduced (nonlinear probes, interventions, latent saliency maps) may prove useful for interpretability in natural language settings.
papers.key_findings:
Othello-GPT predicts legal moves with high accuracy, and this is not due to memorization.
Nonlinear probes can accurately decode the board state from internal activations, while linear probes perform poorly.
Intervention experiments show that the board representation is causal to the model's predictions.
Latent saliency maps reveal differences between models trained on synthetic vs. championship data, indicating different learned strategies.
The internal representation of the board state is nonlinear and emerges during training.
papers.limitation: Latent saliency maps only attribute to one tile when multiple tiles are involved in a move, which does not fully capture the Othello rule logic.
future_direction: Extend investigation to other, more complex games.
Compare strategies learned by a sequence model with those of a model trained with a priori knowledge of Othello.
Study how results generalize to natural language models.
papers.abstract: Language models show a surprising range of capabilities, but the source of their apparent competence is unclear. Do these networks just memorize a collection of surface statistics, or do they rely on internal representations of the process that generates the sequences they see? We investigate this question by applying a variant of the GPT model to the task of predicting legal moves in a simple board game, Othello. Although the network has no a priori knowledge of the game or its rules, we uncover evidence of an emergent nonlinear internal representation of the board state. Interventional experiments indicate this representation can be used to control the output of the network and create "latent saliency maps" that can help explain predictions in human terms.

papers.title: StreetMath: Study of LLMs' Approximation Behaviors
papers.abstract: There is a substantial body of literature examining the mathematical reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), particularly their performance on precise arithmetic operations in autoregressive architectures. However, their ability to perform approximate reasoning in informal, fast-paced mathematical operations has received far less attention, especially among non-autoregressive decoder models. Our work addresses this gap by introducing StreetMath, a benchmark designed to evaluate models' approximation abilities under real-world approximation scenarios. We conduct extensive evaluations across different LLM architectures: Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, Dream-v0-Instruct-7B, Falcon-Mamba-7B-Instruct, and Mamba-GPT-3B. Furthermore, we apply mechanistic interpretability techniques to probe their internal computational states. Our analysis reveals that LLMs generally attempt to compute exact values or invoke external tools even in tasks that call for approximation. Moreover, while models sometimes reach the correct answer in early layers or steps, they still consume more tokens when solving approximation tasks. Additional experiments indicate that exact and approximate arithmetic operations rely on largely separate neural components. Drawing upon research on cognitive psychology, we argue that LLMs do not exhibit cognitive miserliness in the same way humans do in street math settings. We open source our work https://github.com/ctseng777/StreetMath

papers.title: Pre-trained Large Language Models Use Fourier Features to Compute Addition
papers.research_question: How do pre-trained large language models compute addition? The paper shows they use Fourier features in the hidden state.
papers.core_contribution: Pre-trained LLMs compute addition using Fourier features in the hidden state, with MLP layers handling magnitude approximation via low-frequency features and attention layers handling modular addition via high-frequency features. Pre-training provides token embeddings with Fourier features that enable this mechanism.
papers.conclusion: LLMs compute addition by combining approximation and classification via Fourier features, with pre-training being essential for acquiring these features. This suggests that training approaches could be modified to enhance such capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained LLMs progressively compute addition layer by layer, first approximating the answer then refining it.
MLP layers contribute to approximation using low-frequency Fourier features, while attention layers contribute to classification (modular addition) using high-frequency Fourier features.
Pre-trained token embeddings contain Fourier features (periods 2, 5, 10) which are crucial for learning addition.
Models trained from scratch lack Fourier features and achieve lower accuracy; introducing pre-trained token embeddings improves performance.
The same Fourier feature mechanism is observed in prompted pre-trained models (in-context learning).
future_direction: Modifying training approaches to impose constraints that enhance learning of Fourier features for mathematical tasks.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive mathematical reasoning capabilities, yet how they compute basic arithmetic, such as addition, remains unclear. This paper shows that pre-trained LLMs add numbers using Fourier features -- dimensions in the hidden state that represent numbers via a set of features sparse in the frequency domain. Within the model, MLP and attention layers use Fourier features in complementary ways: MLP layers primarily approximate the magnitude of the answer using low-frequency features, while attention layers primarily perform modular addition (e.g., computing whether the answer is even or odd) using high-frequency features. Pre-training is crucial for this mechanism: models trained from scratch to add numbers only exploit low-frequency features, leading to lower accuracy. Introducing pre-trained token embeddings to a randomly initialized model rescues its performance. Overall, our analysis demonstrates that appropriate pre-trained representations (e.g., Fourier features) can unlock the ability of Transformers to learn precise mechanisms for algorithmic tasks.

papers.title: Schema-learning and rebinding as mechanisms of in-context learning and emergence
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning work, and can it be explained through schema-learning and rebinding mechanisms in interpretable models like clone-structured causal graphs (CSCGs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that in-context learning can be achieved through schema-learning and rebinding mechanisms in interpretable clone-structured causal graphs, providing insights into how ICL works in large language models.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that schema-learning and rebinding mechanisms in CSCGs can explain in-context learning, offering insights for designing interpretable architectures and understanding emergence in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
CSCG achieves in-context learning on the GINC dataset, accurately retrieving latent concepts.
CSCG learns template circuits for algorithms and generalizes to novel tokens through rebinding on the LIALT dataset.
ICL performance improves with model overparameterization, suggesting emergence is related to capacity.
CSCG can inductively learn new word usage from single examples in the dax test.
The mechanisms of schema-learning and rebinding in CSCGs provide a plausible explanation for ICL in transformers.
papers.limitation:
CSCG fails to generalize to concepts unseen during training, similar to transformers.
Imperfections in learned CSCG models can lead to failure cases, such as wrong schema retrieval.
future_direction: Designing novel architectures based on schema-learning and rebinding principles.
Searching for interpretable and editable circuits in transformers using the identified mechanisms.
Extending the approach to more complex tasks and datasets.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) is one of the most powerful and most unexpected capabilities to emerge in recent transformer-based large language models (LLMs). Yet the mechanisms that underlie it are poorly understood. In this paper, we demonstrate that comparable ICL capabilities can be acquired by an alternative sequence prediction learning method using clone-structured causal graphs (CSCGs). Moreover, a key property of CSCGs is that, unlike transformer-based LLMs, they are {\em interpretable}, which considerably simplifies the task of explaining how ICL works. Specifically, we show that it uses a combination of (a) learning template (schema) circuits for pattern completion, (b) retrieving relevant templates in a context-sensitive manner, and (c) rebinding of novel tokens to appropriate slots in the templates. We go on to marshall evidence for the hypothesis that similar mechanisms underlie ICL in LLMs. For example, we find that, with CSCGs as with LLMs, different capabilities emerge at different levels of overparameterization, suggesting that overparameterization helps in learning more complex template (schema) circuits. By showing how ICL can be achieved with small models and datasets, we open up a path to novel architectures, and take a vital step towards a more general understanding of the mechanics behind this important capability.

papers.title: Mechanistic Indicators of Understanding in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) possess genuine understanding, and if so, what forms does it take? The paper investigates this by synthesizing findings from mechanistic interpretability within a philosophical framework.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a tiered framework (conceptual, state-of-the-world, principled understanding) for assessing understanding in LLMs and synthesizes mechanistic interpretability evidence to argue that LLMs can develop internal organizations that underwrite understanding-like unification, though these mechanisms diverge from human cognition.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability reveals internal organizations in LLMs that can underwrite understanding-like unification across conceptual, factual, and principled tiers, but these mechanisms diverge from human cognition in their parallel exploitation of heterogeneous, task-specific pathways.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs develop internal 'features' (e.g., a 'Golden Gate Bridge' feature in Claude 3 Sonnet) that act as conceptual unifiers, connecting diverse manifestations of entities or properties.
The linear representation hypothesis is supported, with features encoded as directions in latent space, and superposition allows for efficient representation of many features.
Models like Othello-GPT develop internal 'world models' (e.g., of the board state) that are causally involved in task performance, as shown via probing and intervention techniques.
The phenomenon of 'grokking' demonstrates a shift from memorization to discovering compact, generalizable circuits (e.g., for modular arithmetic), indicative of principled understanding.
Higher-tier understanding mechanisms coexist with lower-tier heuristics (e.g., memorization, n-gram statistics) within LLMs, impacting their epistemic trustworthiness.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often portrayed as merely imitating linguistic patterns without genuine understanding. We argue that recent findings in mechanistic interpretability (MI), the emerging field probing the inner workings of LLMs, render this picture increasingly untenable--but only once those findings are integrated within a theoretical account of understanding. We propose a tiered framework for thinking about understanding in LLMs and use it to synthesize the most relevant findings to date. The framework distinguishes three hierarchical varieties of understanding, each tied to a corresponding level of computational organization: conceptual understanding emerges when a model forms "features" as directions in latent space, learning connections between diverse manifestations of a single entity or property; state-of-the-world understanding emerges when a model learns contingent factual connections between features and dynamically tracks changes in the world; principled understanding emerges when a model ceases to rely on memorized facts and discovers a compact "circuit" connecting these facts. Across these tiers, MI uncovers internal organizations that can underwrite understanding-like unification. However, these also diverge from human cognition in their parallel exploitation of heterogeneous mechanisms. Fusing philosophical theory with mechanistic evidence thus allows us to transcend binary debates over whether AI understands, paving the way for a comparative, mechanistically grounded epistemology that explores how AI understanding aligns with--and diverges from--our own.

papers.title: How Deep is Love in LLMs' Hearts? Exploring Semantic Size in Human-like Cognition
papers.research_question: This study seeks to investigate whether LLMs exhibit similar tendencies in understanding semantic size as humans, thereby providing insights into the underlying mechanisms of human cognition.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that multi-modal training is crucial for LLMs to achieve more human-like understanding of semantic size, and that LLMs, especially multi-modal ones, are influenced by attention-grabbing headlines with larger semantic size, revealing potential biases.
papers.conclusion: The study concludes that multi-modal training enhances LLMs' understanding of semantic size, making them more human-like, but also introduces biases similar to humans, such as susceptibility to clickbait headlines.
papers.key_findings:
Multi-modal LLMs align more closely with human metaphorical tendencies compared to their text-only backbone LLMs.
Multi-modal LLMs outperform single-modality LLMs in semantic size classification accuracy, indicating multi-modality plays a critical role.
LLMs, especially MLLMs, show a clear preference for selecting product titles with larger semantic sizes in a controlled shopping scenario.
The findings suggest that human cognition cannot be fully acquired through the language modality alone; real-world, multi-modal experiences are essential.
Multi-modal training enhances LLMs' ability to understand both abstract and concrete concepts from a semantic size perspective.
papers.abstract: How human cognitive abilities are formed has long captivated researchers. However, a significant challenge lies in developing meaningful methods to measure these complex processes. With the advent of large language models (LLMs), which now rival human capabilities in various domains, we are presented with a unique testbed to investigate human cognition through a new lens. Among the many facets of cognition, one particularly crucial aspect is the concept of semantic size, the perceived magnitude of both abstract and concrete words or concepts. This study seeks to investigate whether LLMs exhibit similar tendencies in understanding semantic size, thereby providing insights into the underlying mechanisms of human cognition. We begin by exploring metaphorical reasoning, comparing how LLMs and humans associate abstract words with concrete objects of varying sizes. Next, we examine LLMs' internal representations to evaluate their alignment with human cognitive processes. Our findings reveal that multi-modal training is crucial for LLMs to achieve more human-like understanding, suggesting that real-world, multi-modal experiences are similarly vital for human cognitive development. Lastly, we examine whether LLMs are influenced by attention-grabbing headlines with larger semantic sizes in a real-world web shopping scenario. The results show that multi-modal LLMs are more emotionally engaged in decision-making, but this also introduces potential biases, such as the risk of manipulation through clickbait headlines. Ultimately, this study offers a novel perspective on how LLMs interpret and internalize language, from the smallest concrete objects to the most profound abstract concepts like love. The insights gained not only improve our understanding of LLMs but also provide new avenues for exploring the cognitive abilities that define human intelligence.

papers.title: Math Neurosurgery: Isolating Language Models' Math Reasoning Abilities Using Only Forward Passes
papers.research_question: How is math reasoning encoded in LLM parameters, and can math-specific parameters be isolated to improve math performance without affecting general language abilities?
papers.core_contribution: MathNeuro is a method to isolate math-specific parameters in LLMs using only forward passes; pruning these parameters deletes math ability without affecting general language, and scaling them improves math performance by 4-35%.
papers.conclusion: MathNeuro successfully isolates math-specific parameters, enabling targeted interventions to enhance math reasoning without compromising other abilities.
papers.key_findings:
MathNeuro isolates math-specific parameters by filtering out parameters important for general language tasks.
Pruning MathNeuro-identified parameters destroys math reasoning ability with minimal impact on non-math tasks.
Scaling these parameters improves math performance by 4-17% on GSM8K and 5-35% on MATH.
MathNeuro is data-efficient, effective even with a single sample.
Math-specific parameters are distributed throughout decoder blocks, not concentrated in specific layers.
future_direction: Applying MathNeuro to other skills or domains
Investigating the impact of different non-math datasets
Studying the theoretical underpinnings
papers.abstract: Math reasoning is an active area of Large Language Model (LLM) research because it is a hallmark of artificial intelligence and has implications in several domains, including math education. However, few works have explored how math reasoning is encoded within LLM parameters and if it is a skill that can be isolated within models. Doing so could allow targeted intervention to improve math performance without altering non-math behavior and foster understanding of how models encode math reasoning. We introduce Math Neurosurgery (MathNeuro), a computationally efficient method we use to isolate math-specific parameters in LLMs using only forward passes. MathNeuro builds on existing work by using weights and activations to calculate parameter importance, but isolates math-specific parameters by filtering out those important for general language tasks. Through pruning parameters MathNeuro identifies, we delete a LLM's math reasoning ability without significantly impacting its general language ability. Scaling the identified parameters by a small constant improves a pretrained or instruction-tuned LLM's performance by 4-17% on GSM8K and 5-35% on MATH while leaving non-math behavior unaltered. MathNeuro is also data efficient: most of its effectiveness holds when identifying math-specific parameters using a single sample. MathNeuro highlights the potential for future work to intervene on math-specific parameters.

papers.title: Low-Complexity Probing via Finding Subnetworks
papers.research_question: Can a subtractive pruning-based probe (subnetwork probing) more faithfully detect linguistic properties encoded in a pre-trained model compared to traditional MLP probes, by being better at finding existing properties and worse at learning tasks on its own?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces subnetwork probing, a pruning-based method that finds a subnetwork within a frozen pre-trained model to perform a linguistic task, demonstrating it is more faithful to the model (higher accuracy on pre-trained, lower on random models) and Pareto-dominates MLP probes in accuracy-complexity tradeoff.
papers.conclusion: Subnetwork probing is a more faithful probing method than existing approaches for understanding what linguistic properties are encoded in pre-trained models, and it enables additional analysis through the subnetworks it discovers.
papers.key_findings:
Subnetwork probing achieves higher accuracy on the pre-trained model and lower accuracy on randomly initialized models compared to an MLP probe, indicating it is better at finding encoded properties and less capable of learning the task independently.
Subnetwork probing Pareto-dominates MLP probing, achieving higher accuracy for any given probe complexity budget.
Analysis of the extracted subnetworks shows that lower-level linguistic tasks (e.g., part-of-speech tagging) are localized in lower layers of the model, reproducing findings from prior work.
future_direction: Applying neuron explainability techniques to the subnetworks discovered by the method.
papers.abstract: The dominant approach in probing neural networks for linguistic properties is to train a new shallow multi-layer perceptron (MLP) on top of the model's internal representations. This approach can detect properties encoded in the model, but at the cost of adding new parameters that may learn the task directly. We instead propose a subtractive pruning-based probe, where we find an existing subnetwork that performs the linguistic task of interest. Compared to an MLP, the subnetwork probe achieves both higher accuracy on pre-trained models and lower accuracy on random models, so it is both better at finding properties of interest and worse at learning on its own. Next, by varying the complexity of each probe, we show that subnetwork probing Pareto-dominates MLP probing in that it achieves higher accuracy given any budget of probe complexity. Finally, we analyze the resulting subnetworks across various tasks to locate where each task is encoded, and we find that lower-level tasks are captured in lower layers, reproducing similar findings in past work.

papers.title: How Pre-trained Word Representations Capture Commonsense Physical Comparisons
papers.research_question: Does pre-trained word representations capture commonsense physical comparisons between objects?
papers.core_contribution: Pre-trained word representations encode commonsense physical comparisons, and a simple probing model using these frozen embeddings achieves higher accuracy than previous methods and generalizes to unseen objects.
papers.conclusion: Pre-trained word representations encode physical commonsense comparisons, and a simple probing model can leverage this with high accuracy and generalization, learning an ordering over objects for comparisons.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained representations (GloVe, ELMo, BERT) capture physical commonsense comparisons with better accuracy than previous approaches.
