papers.abstract: We propose the Quantization Model of neural scaling laws, explaining both the observed power law dropoff of loss with model and data size, and also the sudden emergence of new capabilities with scale. We derive this model from what we call the Quantization Hypothesis, where network knowledge and skills are "quantized" into discrete chunks ($\textbf{quanta}$). We show that when quanta are learned in order of decreasing use frequency, then a power law in use frequencies explains observed power law scaling of loss. We validate this prediction on toy datasets, then study how scaling curves decompose for large language models. Using language model gradients, we automatically decompose model behavior into a diverse set of skills (quanta). We tentatively find that the frequency at which these quanta are used in the training distribution roughly follows a power law corresponding with the empirical scaling exponent for language models, a prediction of our theory.

papers.title: Language Models Do Not Have Human-Like Working Memory
papers.research_question: Can large language models maintain and manipulate unexpressed internal representations (latent state persistence) analogous to human working memory?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs lack the ability to maintain persistent latent states (working memory), functioning instead as reactive post-hoc reasoners, which highlights a fundamental architectural divergence from human-like cognition.
papers.conclusion: Current LLMs lack the ability to persistently maintain and manipulate latent states, functioning as reactive post-hoc reasoners rather than proactive planners, which poses a bottleneck for autonomous agents and tasks requiring working memory.
papers.key_findings:
In the Number Guessing Game, LLMs fail to allocate probability mass to a singular hidden choice, violating the sum-of-probability identity.
In the Yes-No Game, as the number of questions increases, LLMs suffer from concept drift and inevitable self-contradictions due to lack of latent state persistence.
In Mathematical Mentalism, LLMs fail to track transformations on hidden variables, revealing a failure in variable binding and state evolution when the initial state is not explicitly present.
Scaling and long-reasoning traces (e.g., in o3-Mini or DeepSeek-R1) do not bridge the latent state persistence gap; the underlying latent persistence remains absent.
LLMs exhibit human-centric priors such as the 'Blue-Seven' phenomenon, indicating reliance on stochastic priors rather than committed internal states.
papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable reasoning abilities, we demonstrate that they lack a fundamental aspect of human cognition: working memory. Human working memory is an active cognitive system that enables not only the temporary storage of information but also its processing and utilization, enabling coherent reasoning and decision-making. Without working memory, individuals may produce unrealistic responses, exhibit self-contradictions, and struggle with tasks that require mental reasoning. Existing evaluations using N-back or context-dependent tasks fall short as they allow LLMs to exploit external context rather than retaining the reasoning process in the latent space. We introduce three novel tasks: (1) Number Guessing, (2) Yes-No Deduction, and (3) Math Magic, designed to isolate internal representation from external context. Across seventeen frontier models spanning four major model families, we consistently observe irrational or contradictory behaviors, indicating LLMs' inability to retain and manipulate latent information. Our work establishes a new benchmark for evaluating working memory in LLMs and highlights this limitation as a key bottleneck for advancing reliable reasoning systems. Code and prompts for the experiments are available at https://github.com/penguinnnnn/LLM-Working-Memory.

papers.title: LLMs model how humans induce logically structured rules
papers.research_question: Can large language models (LLMs) model human induction of logically structured rules? Do they provide a good fit to human behavior and do they use similar logical or logic-like operators?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs can model human logical rule induction as well as Bayesian probabilistic Language of Thought (pLoT) models, and they may instantiate a novel theoretical account of human logical concepts without built-in logical primitives.
papers.conclusion: LLMs provide a good model of human logical rule induction and may offer a new theoretical account of the primitive representations and computations underlying human logical concepts, with which future work in cognitive science should engage.
papers.key_findings:
Some LLMs (e.g., GPT4, Gemma-7b) achieve human-level accuracy on logical rule induction tasks.
When prompted to explain rules, LLMs sometimes produce rules that use logical operators similar to humans.
Tuning an LLM (Gemma-7b) on human responses yields a better fit to human learning trajectories than tuning on correct answers or than Bayesian pLoT models.
The tuned LLM's high correlation with human data is not just due to learning the rules correctly; it captures human-like learning patterns.
The tuning generalizes to held-out rules and to new rule types (e.g., minority/majority judgments).
papers.limitation:
It is hard to know what the LLM learns when tuning to human responses, and it is hard to fully eliminate the concern that the tuning process is introducing an artifact that increases fit even on withheld exemplars.
The held-out rules share components with seen rules, so generalization might not be fully compositional.
future_direction: Investigate the representations and processes LLMs use for logical rule induction.
Compare LLM-based accounts to human cognitive processes more deeply.
papers.abstract: A central goal of cognitive science is to provide a computationally explicit account of both the structure of the mind and its development: what are the primitive representational building blocks of cognition, what are the rules via which those primitives combine, and where do these primitives and rules come from in the first place? A long-standing debate concerns the adequacy of artificial neural networks as computational models that can answer these questions, in particular in domains related to abstract cognitive function, such as language and logic. This paper argues that recent advances in neural networks -- specifically, the advent of large language models (LLMs) -- represent an important shift in this debate. We test a variety of LLMs on an existing experimental paradigm used for studying the induction of rules formulated over logical concepts. Across four experiments, we find converging empirical evidence that LLMs provide at least as good a fit to human behavior as models that implement a Bayesian probablistic language of thought (pLoT), which have been the best computational models of human behavior on the same task. Moreover, we show that the LLMs make qualitatively different predictions about the nature of the rules that are inferred and deployed in order to complete the task, indicating that the LLM is unlikely to be a mere implementation of the pLoT solution. Based on these results, we argue that LLMs may instantiate a novel theoretical account of the primitive representations and computations necessary to explain human logical concepts, with which future work in cognitive science should engage.

papers.title: Disentangling Polysemantic Neurons with a Null-Calibrated Polysemanticity Index and Causal Patch Interventions
papers.research_question: How can one systematically identify and quantify polysemantic neurons in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Polysemanticity Index (PSI), a null-calibrated metric that combines geometric, categorical, and open-vocabulary semantic evidence to quantify when a neuron's top activations decompose into distinct, nameable concepts.
papers.conclusion: PSI provides a principled and practical tool for discovering, quantifying, and studying polysemantic units in neural networks, and can be extended to benchmark across architectures and training regimes or to study interpretability-performance trade-offs.
papers.key_findings:
PSI robustly distinguishes real neuronal structure from chance, achieving an AUROC of approximately 0.99 when separating late-layer neurons from a null baseline.
Polysemanticity is an emergent property of network depth, with neurons in later layers (layer4) exhibiting significantly higher PSI scores than those in earlier layers (layer3).
Causal patch-swap interventions validate that the feature prototypes discovered by PSI are causally relevant to the neuron's function, with aligned patches increasing activation significantly more than various controls.
PSI rankings are robust to reasonable variations in hyperparameters, such as the number of top patches K, and the optimal number of clusters for decomposable neurons is typically 2 or 3.
The semantic distinctness score (D) is sensitive to the choice of text encoder, indicating that 'semantic distinctness' is relative to the conceptual ontology of the language model used.
papers.limitation:
The open-vocabulary distinctness score (D) is dependent on the chosen multimodal model (CLIP) and its conceptual vocabulary, making semantic distinctness relative to the model's 'conceptual lens'.
The methodology relies on specific choices such as top-K mining (which may miss polysemanticity at moderate activation levels) and K-means clustering (which assumes convex clusters and may not capture complex topological structures).
future_direction: Benchmarking PSI across different architectures and training regimes.
Using PSI as a regularizer to study the trade-off between interpretability and performance.
Extending the PSI approach to analyze neurons or attention heads in large language models (LLMs) or transformers.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often contain polysemantic neurons that respond to multiple, sometimes unrelated, features, complicating mechanistic interpretability. We introduce the Polysemanticity Index (PSI), a null-calibrated metric that quantifies when a neuron's top activations decompose into semantically distinct clusters. PSI multiplies three independently calibrated components: geometric cluster quality (S), alignment to labeled categories (Q), and open-vocabulary semantic distinctness via CLIP (D). On a pretrained ResNet-50 evaluated with Tiny-ImageNet images, PSI identifies neurons whose activation sets split into coherent, nameable prototypes, and reveals strong depth trends: later layers exhibit substantially higher PSI than earlier layers. We validate our approach with robustness checks (varying hyperparameters, random seeds, and cross-encoder text heads), breadth analyses (comparing class-only vs. open-vocabulary concepts), and causal patch-swap interventions. In particular, aligned patch replacements increase target-neuron activation significantly more than non-aligned, random, shuffled-position, or ablate-elsewhere controls. PSI thus offers a principled and practical lever for discovering, quantifying, and studying polysemantic units in neural networks.

papers.title: Diagnostic Classifiers: Revealing how Neural Networks Process Hierarchical Structure
papers.research_question: How do neural networks process hierarchical structure, and what strategies do they use for compositional semantics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces diagnostic classifiers as a method to test hypotheses about the strategies neural networks use, and shows that a GRU follows an incremental strategy for processing hierarchical arithmetic expressions.
papers.conclusion: Diagnostic classifiers are a useful method for understanding how neural networks process hierarchical structure, and the GRU follows an incremental strategy for the arithmetic task.
papers.key_findings:
TreeRNNs can learn to compute the meaning of arithmetic expressions and generalize to longer expressions.
The TreeRNN solution can be understood geometrically through projection, summation, and squashing steps.
GRUs can also learn the task and generalize to longer expressions, but performance deteriorates with length and is worse for right-branching expressions.
Diagnostic classifiers reveal that the GRU follows an incremental strategy rather than a recursive one.
The diagnostic classifier method is a useful tool for analyzing neural network internal dynamics when visualization is insufficient.
papers.limitation:
The TreeRNN requires external parses and is not computationally efficient or biologically plausible.
The GRU's performance deteriorates with sentence length and is worse for right-branching sentences.
The diagnostic classifiers are linear and may not capture all information; the predictions change at every time step while target values remain the same, indicating a possible refinement.
papers.abstract: We investigate how neural networks can be used for hierarchical, compositional semantics. To this end, we define the simple but nontrivial artificial task of processing nested arithmetic expressions and study whether different types of neural networks can learn to add and subtract. We find that recursive neural networks can implement a generalising solution, and we visualise the intermediate steps: projection, summation and squashing. We also show that gated recurrent neural networks, which process the expressions incrementally, perform surprisingly well on this task: they learn to predict the outcome of the arithmetic expressions with reasonable accuracy, although performance deteriorates with increasing length. To analyse what strategy the recurrent network applies, visualisation techniques are less insightful. Therefore, we develop an approach where we formulate and test hypotheses on what strategies these networks might be following. For each hypothesis, we derive predictions about features of the hidden state representations at each time step, and train ’diagnostic classifiers’ to test those predictions. Our results indicate the networks follow a strategy similar to our hypothesised ’incremental strategy’.

papers.title: A Causal Framework to Quantify the Robustness of Mathematical Reasoning with Language Models
papers.research_question: How robust is the mathematical reasoning of language models on math word problems, and what are the causal effects of input factors (e.g., surface form, operands, operators) on the model's solution?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a causal framework to quantify the robustness and sensitivity of language models on math word problems, finding that GPT-3 Davinci models show dramatic improvement in both aspects compared to other GPT variants.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a causal framework for behavioral analysis of language models on math word problems, revealing that robustness does not continuously improve with size, but GPT-3 Davinci models show significant improvement, though performance degrades on more complex problems.
papers.key_findings:
Larger non-instruction-tuned models tend to be more sensitive to changes in the ground-truth result, but not necessarily more robust.
GPT-3 Davinci models (175B) achieve a dramatic improvement in both robustness and sensitivity compared to all other GPT variants.
Instruction tuning (as in GPT-3 Davinci) improves robustness and sensitivity, but the type of instruction tuning matters.
For three-operand problems, even the best models (GPT-3 Davinci) show a significant degradation in robustness.
The causal framework allows disentangling the direct and total causal effects of operands (N) and textual surface form (S) on model predictions.
papers.limitation:
The numerical space for operands is limited to integers up to 300 to ensure numbers are represented as single tokens.
For GPT-3, the API only returns top-k logits, so causal effect metrics (δrcc) are approximated.
The LLaMA tokenizer treats each digit as a separate token, making probability comparison for multi-digit numbers problematic.
future_direction: Examine different types of instruction tuning (e.g., focused on reasoning procedures or reinforcement learning from human feedback).
Extend the framework to more complex problems (e.g., with more operands or different types of math problems).
papers.abstract: We have recently witnessed a number of impressive results on hard mathematical reasoning problems with language models. At the same time, the robustness of these models has also been called into question; recent works have shown that models can rely on shallow patterns in the problem description when generating a solution. Building on the idea of behavioral testing, we propose a novel framework, which pins down the causal effect of various factors in the input, e.g., the surface form of the problem text, the operands, and math operators on the output solution. By grounding the behavioral analysis in a causal graph describing an intuitive reasoning process, we study the behavior of language models in terms of robustness and sensitivity to direct interventions in the input space. We apply our framework on a test bed of math word problems. Our analysis shows that robustness does not appear to continuously improve as a function of size, but the GPT-3 Davinci models (175B) achieve a dramatic improvement in both robustness and sensitivity compared to all other GPT variants.

papers.title: How does Chain of Thought Think? Mechanistic Interpretability of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning with Sparse Autoencoding
papers.research_question: Whether chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting faithfully reflects the true internal reasoning process of large language models.
papers.core_contribution: CoT prompting induces more interpretable, causally effective, and sparser internal features in high-capacity LLMs, enhancing reasoning faithfulness, but this effect is scale-dependent and minimal in smaller models.
papers.conclusion: CoT prompts induce more semantically coherent, causally effective, and sparser internal features in larger LLMs, but these effects are minimal in small models, highlighting the role of model capacity in reasoning faithfulness.
papers.key_findings:
CoT improves feature interpretability and semantic coherence in larger models (Pythia-2.8B) but not in smaller ones (Pythia-70M).
Activation patching shows that CoT features have significant causal efficacy in larger models, improving answer log-probabilities when patched into noCoT runs.
CoT leads to sparser residual activations and SAE feature activations, especially in larger models.
Random feature patching often outperforms top-K patching in large models, indicating that useful CoT information is distributed across many features.
The benefits of CoT are scale-sensitive, with clear effects only in models above a certain size threshold.
papers.limitation:
Activation patching targets only the residual activation of the final token and does not trace causal effects through the reasoning process.
Interpretation module relies on OpenAI's LLM-based scoring, which offers an indirect perspective and is not grounded in specific neurons or heads.
Experiments are restricted to Pythia-2.8B and smaller variants; findings may not generalize to larger models.
SAE-based feature analysis may introduce biases and miss distributed or entangled representations.
future_direction: Conduct token-level and path-based causal analysis, such as stepwise interventions and path patching.
Develop activation-grounded and causally-validated explanation methods, including probing, clustering, and patching.
Scale the framework to larger models and diverse architectures, and explore subspace patching and automated circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting boosts Large Language Models accuracy on multi-step tasks, yet whether the generated "thoughts" reflect the true internal reasoning process is unresolved. We present the first feature-level causal study of CoT faithfulness. Combining sparse autoencoders with activation patching, we extract monosemantic features from Pythia-70M and Pythia-2.8B while they tackle GSM8K math problems under CoT and plain (noCoT) prompting. Swapping a small set of CoT-reasoning features into a noCoT run raises answer log-probabilities significantly in the 2.8B model, but has no reliable effect in 70M, revealing a clear scale threshold. CoT also leads to significantly higher activation sparsity and feature interpretability scores in the larger model, signalling more modular internal computation. For example, the model's confidence in generating correct answers improves from 1.2 to 4.3. We introduce patch-curves and random-feature patching baselines, showing that useful CoT information is not only present in the top-K patches but widely distributed. Overall, our results indicate that CoT can induce more interpretable internal structures in high-capacity LLMs, validating its role as a structured prompting method.

papers.title: Exploring Concept Depth: How Large Language Models Acquire Knowledge and Concept at Different Layers?
papers.research_question: Can shallow layers in LLMs capture meaningful features of simple knowledge, while complex concepts need deeper layers to capture their meaningful features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of 'Concept Depth' to measure how different layers in LLMs capture concepts of varying complexity, showing that simpler concepts are learned in shallow layers while complex concepts require deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: The Concept Depth metric provides a useful framework for understanding how LLMs process concepts of varying complexity across layers, and the experimental insights enhance the understanding of internal representations in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler concepts (e.g., factual knowledge) are learned in shallow layers, while more complex concepts (e.g., reasoning tasks) require deeper layers for accurate understanding.
The pattern of Concept Depth is consistent across different model families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) and model sizes.
Larger models within a family tend to achieve higher peak accuracy and sometimes converge to optimal performance at earlier layers.
Adding noise to the input or quantizing model weights (e.g., to 8-bit) slows down the convergence of concept understanding, requiring deeper layers to achieve comparable accuracy.
Compressing models to 16-bit quantization does not significantly harm the understanding process compared to 32-bit.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performances across a wide range of tasks. However, the mechanisms by which these models encode tasks of varying complexities remain poorly understood. In this paper, we explore the hypothesis that LLMs process concepts of varying complexities in different layers, introducing the idea of "Concept Depth" to suggest that more complex concepts are typically acquired in deeper layers. Specifically, we categorize concepts based on their level of abstraction, defining them in the order of increasing complexity within factual, emotional, and inferential tasks. We conduct extensive probing experiments using layer-wise representations across various LLM families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) on various datasets spanning the three domains of tasks. Our findings reveal that models could efficiently conduct probing for simpler tasks in shallow layers, and more complex tasks typically necessitate deeper layers for accurate understanding. Additionally, we examine how external factors, such as adding noise to the input and quantizing the model weights, might affect layer-wise representations. Our findings suggest that these factors can impede the development of a conceptual understanding of LLMs until deeper layers are explored. We hope that our proposed concept and experimental insights will enhance the understanding of the mechanisms underlying LLMs. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Luckfort/CD.

papers.title: Hierarchical Sparse Circuit Extraction from Billion-Parameter Language Models through Scalable Attribution Graph Decomposition
papers.research_question: How can sparse computational circuits be efficiently extracted from billion-parameter language models using hierarchical decomposition and attribution graphs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Hierarchical Attribution Graph Decomposition (HAGD), a framework that reduces circuit discovery complexity from exponential to polynomial, enabling extraction of interpretable circuits from billion-parameter models with high behavioral preservation.
papers.conclusion: HAGD enables circuit extraction from large models with preserved behavior, but limitations include incomplete attention modeling, reconstruction residuals, and interpretability challenges for large circuits.
papers.key_findings:
HAGD reduces circuit discovery complexity to O(n^2 log n) and extracts circuits from models up to 70B parameters.
Behavioral preservation ranges from 82% to 97% on algorithmic tasks and 74% to 88% on natural language benchmarks.
Cross-architecture transfer shows 52%-82% structural similarity, indicating shared computational patterns.
Circuit size grows sublinearly with model parameters, but natural language tasks yield larger, less modular circuits.
The method outperforms baselines like ACDC in scalability while maintaining comparable circuit quality.
papers.limitation:
Attention circuits are not modeled, leaving significant computational pathways unanalyzed.
Reconstruction dark matter of 15-20% unexplained variance means extracted circuits are incomplete.
Validation circularity arises from using ablation experiments that assume circuit completeness.
GNN meta-model requires ground-truth circuit labels that are expensive to obtain.
Large circuits with hundreds of nodes may exceed human interpretability limits.
future_direction: Integrate attention and MLP circuit analysis.
Characterize reconstruction residuals (dark matter).
Develop label-efficient training methods for GNN meta-model.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to reverse-engineer neural network computations into human-understandable algorithms, yet extracting sparse computational circuits from billion-parameter language models remains challenging due to exponential search complexity and pervasive polysemanticity. The proposed Hierarchical Attribution Graph Decomposition (HAGD) framework reduces circuit discovery complexity from O(2^n) exhaustive enumeration to O(n^2 log n) through multi-resolution abstraction hierarchies and differentiable circuit search. The methodology integrates cross-layer transcoders for monosemantic feature extraction, graph neural network meta-learning for topology prediction, and causal intervention protocols for validation. Empirical evaluation spans GPT-2 variants, Llama-7B through Llama-70B, and Pythia suite models across algorithmic tasks and natural language benchmarks. On modular arithmetic tasks, the framework achieves up to 91% behavioral preservation ($\pm$2.3\% across runs) while maintaining interpretable subgraph sizes. Cross-architecture transfer experiments suggest that discovered circuits exhibit moderate structural similarity (averaging 67%) across model families, indicating potential shared computational patterns. These results provide preliminary foundations for interpretability at larger model scales while identifying significant limitations in current attribution methodologies that require future advances.

papers.title: The LLM Language Network: A Neuroscientific Approach for Identifying Causally Task-Relevant Units
papers.research_question: Does specialization for language (and other cognitive domains) emerge in large language models, and what is the causal role of such specialized units?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired method to identify language-selective units in LLMs and demonstrates their causal role in language processing through ablation studies.
papers.conclusion: LLMs develop specialized language units that are causally important for language processing, similar to the human brain, but specialization for other cognitive domains is less consistent.
papers.key_findings:
Language-selective units can be identified in LLMs using the same functional localization method as in neuroscience.
Ablating even a small percentage (e.g., 1%) of language-selective units causes significant performance drops in language tasks, while ablating random units does not.
The language-selective units in LLMs show similar response profiles to the human language network (e.g., stronger responses to sentences than to non-words, arithmetic, or code).
The language-selective units are more aligned to brain recordings from the human language network than random units, especially when selecting a small subset of units.
Specialization for other cognitive domains (reasoning and theory of mind) is not consistently found across LLMs, with only a subset of models showing such specialization.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focused on models smaller than 13 billion parameters, which may not capture specialization in larger models.
They evaluated Theory of Mind and Multiple Demand units using only one benchmark each (TOMi for ToM and MATH for MD), which may not be comprehensive.
The localizers are adapted from neuroscience and may be constrained by the stimuli sets traditionally used in neuroscience.
future_direction: Expanding the study to include more models and a broader set of benchmarks.
Developing more targeted and robust localizers not restricted by neuroscience stimuli.
Analyzing varying numbers of selective units for MD and ToM networks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities on not just language tasks, but also various tasks that are not linguistic in nature, such as logical reasoning and social inference. In the human brain, neuroscience has identified a core language system that selectively and causally supports language processing. We here ask whether similar specialization for language emerges in LLMs. We identify language-selective units within 18 popular LLMs, using the same localization approach that is used in neuroscience. We then establish the causal role of these units by demonstrating that ablating LLM language-selective units -- but not random units -- leads to drastic deficits in language tasks. Correspondingly, language-selective LLM units are more aligned to brain recordings from the human language system than random units. Finally, we investigate whether our localization method extends to other cognitive domains: while we find specialized networks in some LLMs for reasoning and social capabilities, there are substantial differences among models. These findings provide functional and causal evidence for specialization in large language models, and highlight parallels with the functional organization in the brain.

papers.title: A simple probabilistic neural network for machine understanding
papers.research_question: What are the properties of learning machines with a fixed internal representation, derived from principles of maximal relevance and maximal ignorance, in unsupervised learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Hierarchical Feature Model (HFM), a probabilistic neural network with a fixed internal representation derived from principles of maximal relevance and maximal ignorance, and shows that it has desirable properties like continuity, controllable compression, and ability to support functions beyond generalization.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that learning machines with a fixed internal representation, such as the HFM, operate in a qualitatively different regime from traditional models like RBMs, with data-specific information stored in weights and potential for higher cognitive functions.
papers.key_findings:
The HFM is uniquely identified by the principles of maximal relevance and maximal ignorance when hidden units are binary.
The HFM exhibits a phase transition at a critical coupling parameter g, with a divergence in specific heat.
Training the HFM with an EM algorithm allows features to be learned sequentially, with low-order features remaining stable as new features are added.
The internal representation of the HFM is robust to changes in the coupling parameter and dataset size, and low-order features capture most of the relevant information.
The learning modality of HFM is qualitatively different from RBMs: in HFM, data-specific information is stored in the weights, while in RBMs it is transferred to the internal representation.
future_direction: Investigating whether a universal data-independent internal representation emerges spontaneously in deep layers of learning architectures.
Relating the findings to thermodynamic costs of learning.
Exploring the hypothesis that internal representations evolve with depth in hierarchical learning systems.
papers.abstract: We discuss probabilistic neural networks with a fixed internal representation as models for machine understanding. Here understanding is intended as mapping data to an already existing representation which encodes an {\em a priori} organisation of the feature space. We derive the internal representation by requiring that it satisfies the principles of maximal relevance and of maximal ignorance about how different features are combined. We show that, when hidden units are binary variables, these two principles identify a unique model -- the Hierarchical Feature Model (HFM) -- which is fully solvable and provides a natural interpretation in terms of features. We argue that learning machines with this architecture enjoy a number of interesting properties, like the continuity of the representation with respect to changes in parameters and data, the possibility to control the level of compression and the ability to support functions that go beyond generalisation. We explore the behaviour of the model with extensive numerical experiments and argue that models where the internal representation is fixed reproduce a learning modality which is qualitatively different from that of traditional models such as Restricted Boltzmann Machines.

papers.title: Levels of Analysis for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can methods from cognitive science, particularly David Marr's levels of analysis, be used to understand large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework for understanding large language models by applying David Marr's three levels of analysis (computational, algorithmic, implementation) from cognitive science, and surveys established cognitive science techniques relevant to each level.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the levels of analysis framework and the toolkit of cognitive science methods provide a valuable approach for understanding the behavior and internal organization of large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Large language models exhibit 'embers of autoregression'—behavioral trends that reflect their next-token prediction training objective, even in deterministic tasks.
LLMs show systematic deviations from normative benchmarks such as the axioms of probability theory, similar to human biases.
Methods from cognitive psychology, such as adapted implicit association tests, can reveal hidden associations in value-aligned LLMs that are not apparent in direct questioning.
At the implementation level, techniques like activation patching and circuit discovery can identify causal mechanisms within the model's architecture.
The levels of analysis framework provides a structured toolkit for making sense of LLMs by connecting their function, algorithms, and physical implementation.
papers.abstract: Modern artificial intelligence systems, such as large language models, are increasingly powerful but also increasingly hard to understand. Recognizing this problem as analogous to the historical difficulties in understanding the human mind, we argue that methods developed in cognitive science can be useful for understanding large language models. We propose a framework for applying these methods based on the levels of analysis that David Marr proposed for studying information processing systems. By revisiting established cognitive science techniques relevant to each level and illustrating their potential to yield insights into the behavior and internal organization of large language models, we aim to provide a toolkit for making sense of these new kinds of minds.

papers.title: Finite State Automata Inside Transformers with Chain-of-Thought: A Mechanistic Study on State Tracking
papers.research_question: Does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) help transformers recover a world model in the form of finite state automata (FSAs), or do they merely learn shortcuts?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer+CoT learns implicit finite state automata (FSAs) for state tracking, as evidenced by mechanistic analysis showing that late-layer MLP neurons implement state transitions and exhibit compression and distinction properties.
papers.conclusion: Transformer+CoT achieves near-perfect next-token prediction while internalizing an FSA-like structured state representation, bridging the gap between theoretical expressiveness and practical learnability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer+CoT efficiently learns state tracking for sequences of arbitrary length across multiple groups (Z60, A4 × Z5, A5), outperforming other architectures like RNNs and transformer variants.
The circuit for state tracking relies heavily on late-layer MLP neurons, with MLP11 playing a key role.
Neurons in late-layer MLPs can be classified into states based on transition rules with high accuracy, indicating an N-to-1 mapping between neurons and states.
The model exhibits near-perfect compression and distinction metrics, providing evidence that it recovers an implicit FSA structure.
The learned FSAs are robust to skipping intermediate steps and noise in scratchpads, but struggle with generalization to significantly longer sequences.
papers.limitation: The model struggles with generalization to significantly longer sequences.
future_direction: Modifications to model architecture, loss functions, or optimization algorithms to improve length generalization.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) significantly enhances the performance of large language models (LLMs) across a wide range of tasks, and prior research shows that CoT can theoretically increase expressiveness. However, there is limited mechanistic understanding of the algorithms that Transformer+CoT can learn. Our key contributions are: (1) We evaluate the state tracking capabilities of Transformer+CoT and its variants, confirming the effectiveness of CoT. (2) Next, we identify the circuit (a subset of model components, responsible for tracking the world state), indicating that late-layer MLP neurons play a key role. We propose two metrics, compression and distinction, and show that the neuron sets for each state achieve nearly 100% accuracy, providing evidence of an implicit finite state automaton (FSA) embedded within the model. (3) Additionally, we explore three challenging settings: skipping intermediate steps, introducing data noises, and testing length generalization. Our results demonstrate that Transformer+CoT learns robust algorithms (FSAs), highlighting its resilience in challenging scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/IvanChangPKU/FSA.

papers.title: Emergent Symbol-like Number Variables in Artificial Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What types of numeric representations emerge in neural systems, and how can we interpret neural network solutions through the lens of interpretable Symbolic Algorithms?
papers.core_contribution: We extend the Distributed Alignment Search framework with alignment functions to interpret neural network activity in terms of symbolic variables, and show that recurrent networks develop graded symbol-like number variables while transformers use anti-Markovian solutions.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates the utility of causal interpretability tools and alignment functions for understanding neural representations, showing that RNNs develop graded symbol-like number variables while transformers use anti-Markovian solutions.
papers.key_findings:
Recurrent models (GRUs/LSTMs) develop graded symbol-like number variables within their neural activity.
Seemingly insignificant task variations can drastically affect alignment to Symbolic Algorithms, motivating extended DAS with alignment functions (LAFs).
Linear Alignment Functions (LAFs) can control NN behavior through neural activity aligned to interpretable Symbolic Algorithms.
Shallow Transformers use anti-Markovian solutions to numeric tasks, and theoretically, Transformers must use anti-Markovian solutions without sufficient attention layers.
Causal interventions on neural subspaces are useful for NN interpretability.
papers.abstract: What types of numeric representations emerge in neural systems, and what would a satisfying answer to this question look like? In this work, we interpret Neural Network (NN) solutions to sequence based number tasks using a variety of methods to understand how well we can interpret them through the lens of interpretable Symbolic Algorithms (SAs) -- precise programs describable by rules and typed, mutable variables. We use autoregressive GRUs, LSTMs, and Transformers trained on tasks where the correct tokens depend on numeric information only latent in the task structure. We show through multiple causal and theoretical methods that we can interpret raw NN activity through the lens of simplified SAs when we frame the activity in terms of neural subspaces rather than individual neurons. Using Distributed Alignment Search (DAS), we find that, depending on network architecture, dimensionality, and task specifications, alignments with SA's can be very high, or they can be only approximate, or fail altogether. We extend our analytic toolkit to address the failure cases by expanding the DAS framework to a broader class of alignment functions that more flexibly capture NN activity in terms of interpretable variables from SAs, and we provide theoretic and empirical explorations of Linear Alignment Functions (LAFs) in contrast to the preexisting Orthogonal Alignment Functions (OAFs). Through analyses of specific cases we confirm the usefulness of causal interventions on neural subspaces for NN interpretability, and we show that recurrent models can develop graded, symbol-like number variables in their neural activity. We further show that shallow Transformers learn very different solutions than recurrent networks, and we prove that such models must use anti-Markovian solutions -- solutions that do not rely on cumulative, Markovian hidden states -- in the absence of sufficient attention layers.

papers.title: Think-to-Talk or Talk-to-Think? When LLMs Come Up with an Answer in Multi-Hop Arithmetic Reasoning
papers.research_question: When during chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning do LLMs determine their final answer, and how causally dependent is the answer on the CoT explanation?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs compute answers iteratively during CoT generation, and the CoT explanations are faithful reflections of their internal computation, not post-hoc justifications.
papers.conclusion: LLMs compute answers iteratively during CoT, making CoT explanations faithful to the internal reasoning process.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not determine the final answer before CoT begins; instead, they compute sub-answers during CoT generation.
Linear probes show that answers become linearly separable in hidden states only after corresponding reasoning steps in CoT.
Causal interventions show that the final answer depends causally on the CoT part, especially the latter steps, showing recency bias.
The model's internal reasoning follows a recency bias: each step causally depends on the previous step.
For distractors (unnecessary variables), the model does not encode them in a linearly separable form, indicating efficient internal mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
The study uses synthetic arithmetic tasks, which may not generalize to natural language reasoning.
The cause of incorrect answers in some instances remains unclear.
future_direction: Investigate more complex and natural language reasoning tasks.
Detailed analysis of error cases and internal representations of digits.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the incremental, internal problem-solving process of language models (LMs) with arithmetic multi-hop reasoning as a case study. We specifically investigate when LMs internally resolve sub/whole problems through first reading the problem statements, generating reasoning chains, and achieving the final answer to mechanistically interpret LMs' multi-hop problem-solving process. Our experiments reveal a systematic incremental reasoning strategy underlying LMs. They have not derived an answer at the moment they first read the problem; instead, they obtain (sub)answers while generating the reasoning chain. Therefore, the generated reasoning chains can be regarded as faithful reflections of the model's internal computation.

papers.title: Algorithmic Phase Transitions in Language Models: A Mechanistic Case Study of Arithmetic
papers.research_question: How do language models achieve zero-shot performance on some tasks but not others? Specifically, do they use stable algorithms across related subtasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concepts of algorithmic stability and algorithmic phase transitions, and shows that language models exhibit sharp algorithmic phase transitions even on simple arithmetic tasks, which may explain poor generalization.
papers.conclusion: Language models are algorithmically unstable for two-operand addition, and this instability may be a barrier for generalization in logical reasoning. The introduced interpretability technique can help evaluate model design choices and serve as a diagnostic tool.
papers.key_findings:
Gemma-2-2b uses different computational subcircuits for addition problems with different digit lengths, indicating algorithmic instability.
The model undergoes sharp algorithmic phase transitions between symmetric, boundary, and interior addition tasks.
The structure of the identified subcircuits varies: symmetric tasks show top-heavy circuits, boundary tasks show two peaks of activation, and interior tasks show diffuse circuits.
Algorithmic instability correlates with lack of generalization in arithmetic performance.
The paper introduces methods to quantify algorithmic changes using activation patching and clustering techniques.
papers.limitation:
Relies on activation patching, which has known limitations.
Operationalizes algorithmic changes as structural changes, which may not capture all aspects of algorithmic change.
future_direction: Test the robustness of identified subcircuits by perturbing the weights of the network.
Explore other methods to quantify algorithmic changes beyond structural similarity.
papers.abstract: Zero-shot capabilities of large language models make them powerful tools for solving a range of tasks without explicit training. It remains unclear, however, how these models achieve such performance, or why they can zero-shot some tasks but not others. In this paper, we shed some light on this phenomenon by defining and investigating algorithmic stability in language models -- changes in problem-solving strategy employed by the model as a result of changes in task specification. We focus on a task where algorithmic stability is needed for generalization: two-operand arithmetic. Surprisingly, we find that Gemma-2-2b employs substantially different computational models on closely related subtasks, i.e. four-digit versus eight-digit addition. Our findings suggest that algorithmic instability may be a contributing factor to language models' poor zero-shot performance across certain logical reasoning tasks, as they struggle to abstract different problem-solving strategies and smoothly transition between them.

papers.title: Vector Symbolic Architectures answer Jackendoff's challenges for cognitive neuroscience
papers.research_question: Can Vector Symbolic Architectures meet Jackendoff's four challenges for cognitive neuroscience?
papers.core_contribution: Vector Symbolic Architectures can meet Jackendoff's four challenges for cognitive neuroscience, providing a connectionist basis for symbolic processing.
papers.conclusion: Vector Symbolic Architectures meet Jackendoff's challenges due to their algebraic properties and straightforward physical implementations, but they are relatively unknown because they depend on good design rather than training.
papers.key_findings:
VSAs address the binding problem by using elementwise multiplication for binding, allowing fast construction of novel composite structures.
VSAs handle multiple instances of the same token through superposition and binding with distinct attributes, using frame-like representations.
VSAs implement variables and substitutions through binding operations, enabling productive language rules.
VSAs represent working memory and long-term memory with the same vector dimensionality, making the boundary between them transparent.
VSAs are suitable for cognitive modelling but require good design rather than automated training, making them difficult to work with at higher architectural levels.
papers.limitation:
There is no currently available representational architecture and cognitive architecture that implements fully variable, input driven composition.
VSAs are very difficult to work with at the level of complete representational architectures and cognitive architectures, requiring good design rather than automated training.
future_direction: Developing enhanced recurrent associative memories that can recognize novel composites by retrieving components and generating mappings.
Extending VSA analysis to the representational and cognitive architecture levels.
papers.abstract: Jackendoff (2002) posed four challenges that linguistic combinatoriality and rules of language present to theories of brain function. The essence of these problems is the question of how to neurally instantiate the rapid construction and transformation of the compositional structures that are typically taken to be the domain of symbolic processing. He contended that typical connectionist approaches fail to meet these challenges and that the dialogue between linguistic theory and cognitive neuroscience will be relatively unproductive until the importance of these problems is widely recognised and the challenges answered by some technical innovation in connectionist modelling. This paper claims that a little-known family of connectionist models (Vector Symbolic Architectures) are able to meet Jackendoff's challenges.

papers.title: Decoding In-Context Learning: Neuroscience-inspired Analysis of Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context learning, and how do these changes mediate improvement in behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired framework using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Attention Ratio Analysis (ARA) to show that in-context learning improves task-critical representations and attention allocation, which correlate with behavioral gains.
papers.conclusion: ICL improves task-critical representations and attention allocation to relevant content in the prompt, and these representational changes are correlated with behavioral gains.
papers.key_findings:
ICL leads to changes in prompt embedding similarity matrices to better encode task-critical information, which in turn improves behavior.
ICL increases the decodability of task-critical information (e.g., line slope) from embeddings via probing classifiers.
ICL shifts attention to relevant content in the prompt (increased attention ratio to informative parts), which correlates with behavioral improvement.
These representational changes are consistent across multiple layers (except the first) in both Llama-2 and Vicuna models.
The proposed methods (RSA and ARA) provide scalable tools for analyzing latent representations in large language models.
future_direction: Study the effects of ICL on improving planning behavior in LLMs by analyzing latent representations before and after ICL in planning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable performance improvement through in-context learning (ICL) by leveraging task-specific examples in the input. However, the mechanisms behind this improvement remain elusive. In this work, we investigate how LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context-learning, and how these changes mediate improvement in behavior. We employ neuroscience-inspired techniques such as representational similarity analysis (RSA) and propose novel methods for parameterized probing and measuring ratio of attention to relevant vs. irrelevant information in Llama-2 70B and Vicuna 13B. We designed two tasks with a priori relationships among their conditions: linear regression and reading comprehension. We formed hypotheses about expected similarities in task representations and measured hypothesis alignment of LLM representations before and after ICL as well as changes in attention. Our analyses revealed a meaningful correlation between improvements in behavior after ICL and changes in both embeddings and attention weights across LLM layers. This empirical framework empowers a nuanced understanding of how latent representations shape LLM behavior, offering valuable tools and insights for future research and practical applications.

papers.title: Bridging the Knowledge-Prediction Gap in LLMs on Multiple-Choice Questions
papers.research_question: What is the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs on multiple-choice questions and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a geometric interpretation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs and introduces KAPPA, an inference-time intervention that aligns knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream to mitigate the gap.
papers.conclusion: The knowledge-prediction gap is a pervasive phenomenon in LLMs, and representation-level alignment via methods like KAPPA can elicit more faithful predictions.
papers.key_findings:
The knowledge-prediction gap is widespread across diverse MCQ benchmarks and model families.
The gap can be geometrically interpreted as a misalignment between knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream.
KAPPA effectively reduces the gap and improves accuracy across benchmarks without additional training.
The gap is more pronounced in reasoning, truthfulness, and bias benchmarks compared to knowledge-intensive benchmarks.
The identified subspaces partially transfer across tasks requiring similar skills.
papers.limitation: The method relies on linearly accessible knowledge, leaving nonlinearly encoded knowledge unexplored.
future_direction: Developing more reliable methods to extract knowledge from model representations.
Understanding how nonlinearly encoded knowledge can be aligned.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on diverse tasks, their trustworthiness is limited by erratic behavior that is unfaithful to their internal knowledge. In particular, LLMs often fail on multiple-choice questions (MCQs) even if they encode correct answers in their hidden representations, revealing a misalignment between internal knowledge and output behavior. We investigate and mitigate this knowledge-prediction gap on MCQs through a three-step analysis of hidden representations. First, we quantify the prevalence and magnitude of the gap across models and datasets. Second, we provide a geometric interpretation by identifying distinct knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream. Third, we introduce KAPPA, a lightweight inference-time intervention that aligns the two subspaces within the residual stream to reduce the knowledge-prediction gap. Our results provide a geometric and interpretable explanation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs. Furthermore, KAPPA effectively reduces the gap across diverse MCQ benchmarks and models, and generalizes to free-form settings.

papers.title: In-Context Algebra
papers.research_question: What computational strategies do transformers develop when tokens serve as pure variables, acquiring meaning only through their interactions within each sequence, rather than relying on fixed information encoded in token embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained on an in-context variable assignment task develop symbolic reasoning mechanisms (commutative copying, identity element recognition, closure-based cancellation) that differ from the geometric representations learned in fixed-token arithmetic settings, showing that learned reasoning strategies depend on task structure.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can develop symbolic reasoning mechanisms when trained to reason in-context about variables whose meanings are not fixed, showing that the kinds of learned strategies are dependent on the task structure.
papers.key_findings:
Models learn a commutative copying mechanism where a dedicated attention head copies answers from previously seen commutative facts.
Models develop an identity element recognition mechanism that distinguishes and solves facts containing the group's identity element.
Models implement a closure-based cancellation mechanism that tracks group membership to constrain valid answers by eliminating impossible variables.
The reasoning strategies learned by transformers are dependent on the task structure, with symbolic, context-based strategies emerging when tokens carry no consistent meaning across contexts.
Models achieve near-perfect accuracy on the task and generalize to unseen groups.
papers.limitation: The study is conducted on synthetic algebra tasks with small transformer models, which may limit generalizability to larger models or more complex, real-world reasoning tasks.
future_direction: Exploring more complex algebraic structures and reasoning tasks.
Scaling the analysis to larger transformer models.
Investigating whether similar symbolic mechanisms emerge in other in-context learning settings.
papers.abstract: We investigate the mechanisms that arise when transformers are trained to solve arithmetic on sequences where tokens are variables whose meaning is determined only through their interactions. While prior work has found that transformers develop geometric embeddings that mirror algebraic structure, those previous findings emerge from settings where arithmetic-valued tokens have fixed meanings. We devise a new task in which the assignment of symbols to specific algebraic group elements varies from one sequence to another. Despite this challenging setup, transformers achieve near-perfect accuracy on the task and even generalize to unseen algebraic groups. We develop targeted data distributions to create causal tests of a set of hypothesized mechanisms, and we isolate three mechanisms models consistently learn: commutative copying where a dedicated head copies answers, identity element recognition that distinguishes identity-containing facts, and closure-based cancellation that tracks group membership to constrain valid answers. Complementary to the geometric representations found in fixed-symbol settings, our findings show that models develop symbolic reasoning mechanisms when trained to reason in-context with variables whose meanings are not fixed.

papers.title: A Relational Inductive Bias for Dimensional Abstraction in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What is the impact of a relational bottleneck on the learning of factorized representations and generalization in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The relational bottleneck inductive bias promotes learning of factorized representations, improving generalization efficiency and aligning network behavior with human cognitive biases.
papers.conclusion: The relational bottleneck induces factorized, compositional representations that approximate human coding efficiency and processing flexibility.
papers.key_findings:
Relational networks learn faster and achieve better out-of-distribution generalization than standard feedforward networks.
Relational networks develop orthogonal, factorized representations of feature dimensions in their embeddings.
Relational networks reproduce human-like regularity biases in geometric oddball detection tasks.
Relational networks show more robust representation of stimulus regularity compared to standard contrastive models like SimCLR.
The benefits of relational processing extend to various tasks including visual reasoning and analogy.
papers.abstract: The human cognitive system exhibits remarkable flexibility and generalization capabilities, partly due to its ability to form low-dimensional, compositional representations of the environment. In contrast, standard neural network architectures often struggle with abstract reasoning tasks, overfitting, and requiring extensive data for training. This paper investigates the impact of the relational bottleneck -- a mechanism that focuses processing on relations among inputs -- on the learning of factorized representations conducive to compositional coding and the attendant flexibility of processing. We demonstrate that such a bottleneck not only improves generalization and learning efficiency, but also aligns network performance with human-like behavioral biases. Networks trained with the relational bottleneck developed orthogonal representations of feature dimensions latent in the dataset, reflecting the factorized structure thought to underlie human cognitive flexibility. Moreover, the relational network mimics human biases towards regularity without pre-specified symbolic primitives, suggesting that the bottleneck fosters the emergence of abstract representations that confer flexibility akin to symbols.

papers.title: Exposing Attention Glitches with Flip-Flop Language Modeling
papers.research_question: Why do large language models sometimes output factual inaccuracies and exhibit erroneous reasoning? The paper investigates the phenomenon of attention glitches as a potential cause.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and analyzes the phenomenon of attention glitches in Transformers, introduces flip-flop language modeling (FFLM) as a synthetic benchmark to isolate these errors, and finds that Transformers exhibit a long tail of sporadic reasoning errors even on this simple task.
papers.conclusion: Attention glitches are a fundamental failure mode of Transformer architectures when processing long-range dependencies, and may account for some closed-domain hallucinations in natural language models.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers exhibit a long, irregular tail of reasoning errors (attention glitches) on flip-flop language modeling, while LSTMs extrapolate perfectly.
Natural language models (e.g., GPT-4, Pythia) can process flip-flop languages but not robustly, with error rates amplifying with sequence length.
Training on out-of-distribution data (rare sequences) significantly reduces errors, more so than scaling model size or training data.
Attention-sharpening regularizers reduce reasoning errors by an order of magnitude by promoting sparse attention patterns.
No mitigation tried (including regularization, architecture changes, and scaling) completely eliminated attention glitches.
papers.limitation:
None of the attempted mitigations (regularization, architecture changes, scaling) were successful in driving the number of errors to exactly zero.
Attention patterns may not be fully reliable for interpretability, as they can interact with other components in non-intuitive ways.
future_direction: A more thorough study of the training dynamics of flip-flop tasks with attention-sharpening regularization.
Understanding how to build robust Transformer models and training pipelines at larger scales.
Investigating the connection between attention glitches and closed-domain hallucinations in natural language models.
papers.abstract: Why do large language models sometimes output factual inaccuracies and exhibit erroneous reasoning? The brittleness of these models, particularly when executing long chains of reasoning, currently seems to be an inevitable price to pay for their advanced capabilities of coherently synthesizing knowledge, pragmatics, and abstract thought. Towards making sense of this fundamentally unsolved problem, this work identifies and analyzes the phenomenon of attention glitches, in which the Transformer architecture's inductive biases intermittently fail to capture robust reasoning. To isolate the issue, we introduce flip-flop language modeling (FFLM), a parametric family of synthetic benchmarks designed to probe the extrapolative behavior of neural language models. This simple generative task requires a model to copy binary symbols over long-range dependencies, ignoring the tokens in between. We find that Transformer FFLMs suffer from a long tail of sporadic reasoning errors, some of which we can eliminate using various regularization techniques. Our preliminary mechanistic analyses show why the remaining errors may be very difficult to diagnose and resolve. We hypothesize that attention glitches account for (some of) the closed-domain hallucinations in natural LLMs.

papers.title: It Ain't That Bad: Understanding the Mysterious Performance Drop in OOD Generalization for Generative Transformer Models
papers.research_question: Why do generative transformer models exhibit strong in-distribution generalization but poor out-of-distribution generalization on arithmetic tasks, and is there a systematic pattern behind the OOD failures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that generative transformer models trained on n-digit arithmetic operations learn to map out-of-distribution inputs to outputs via equivalence classes modulo 10^n, explaining their poor OOD performance as systematic rather than random errors.
papers.conclusion: Generative transformer models exhibit equivalence generalization, mapping OOD inputs to ID equivalence classes, and representation learning plays a crucial role in both ID and OOD generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Models achieve near-perfect ID generalization but zero OOD accuracy on longer-digit arithmetic tasks.
The models learn an algebraic structure: they map OOD inputs to outputs by taking the operands modulo 10^n (for n-digit training), a phenomenon termed equivalence generalization.
Equivalence generalization is robust across different encoding methods, training data variations, and model scales.
Representation learning evolves from random to structured, enabling ID generalization but leading to systematic errors in OOD.
Increasing model size does not improve length generalization ability.
papers.limitation: The findings are based on synthetic arithmetic tasks and may not directly translate to natural language tasks due to the subjectivity and complexity of language.
future_direction: Using equivalence generalization as prior knowledge to guide training and reduce data needs
Applying equivalence class similarity metrics to domain adaptation for OOD generalization
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable proficiency on solving diverse problems. However, their generalization ability is not always satisfying and the generalization problem is common for generative transformer models in general. Researchers take basic mathematical tasks like n-digit addition or multiplication as important perspectives for investigating their generalization behaviors. It is observed that when training models on n-digit operations (e.g., additions) in which both input operands are n-digit in length, models generalize successfully on unseen n-digit inputs (in-distribution (ID) generalization), but fail miserably on longer, unseen cases (out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization). We bring this unexplained performance drop into attention and ask whether there is systematic OOD generalization. Towards understanding LLMs, we train various smaller language models which may share the same underlying mechanism. We discover that the strong ID generalization stems from structured representations, while behind the unsatisfying OOD performance, the models still exhibit clear learned algebraic structures. Specifically, these models map unseen OOD inputs to outputs with learned equivalence relations in the ID domain, which we call the equivalence generalization. These findings deepen our knowledge regarding the generalizability of generative models including LLMs, and provide insights into potential avenues for improvement.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Fine-Tuning Mechanisms of LLMs via Circuit Analysis
papers.research_question: How do circuits in LLMs evolve during fine-tuning, and can insights from circuit analysis be used to improve the fine-tuning process?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that fine-tuning primarily modifies edges in circuits rather than nodes, and uses this insight to develop CircuitLoRA, a circuit-aware LoRA method that improves accuracy and parameter efficiency.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning primarily modifies edges rather than merely introducing new components to form new circuits. Building on this insight, the developed circuit-aware LoRA method enhances fine-tuning efficiency, and the composition of subtask circuits effectively represents the circuit of a compositional task.
papers.key_findings:
Circuits can be identified in both pre-trained and fine-tuned models with high faithfulness and robustness, regardless of their significant performance differences.
Fine-tuning performs more significant edge modifications than node modifications.
Circuits can in turn improve fine-tuning with higher accuracy and parameter efficiency across various mathematical tasks.
The composition of the circuits can effectively represent the circuits of the compositional task.
papers.limitation:
The work focused on math tasks, so applying circuit-based methods to more tasks would further validate the generality of the insights.
The compositional experiments only explore two-step arithmetic, limiting insights into more complex multi-step tasks.
future_direction: Applying circuit-based methods to more tasks to validate the generality of the insights.
Extending the analysis of compositional tasks to multi-step or more complex tasks to provide deeper insights into circuit interactions.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning significantly improves the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. This paper aims to provide an in-depth interpretation of the fine-tuning process through circuit analysis, a popular tool in Mechanistic Interpretability (MI). Unlike previous studies (Prakash et al. 2024; Chhabra et al. 2024) that focus on tasks where pre-trained models already perform well, we develop a set of mathematical tasks where fine-tuning yields substantial performance gains, which are closer to the practical setting. In our experiments, we identify circuits at various checkpoints during fine-tuning and examine the interplay between circuit analysis, fine-tuning methods, and task complexities. First, we find that while circuits maintain high node similarity before and after fine-tuning, their edges undergo significant changes, in contrast to prior work that shows circuits only add some additional components after fine-tuning. Based on these observations, we develop a circuit-aware Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) method, which assigns ranks to layers based on edge changes in the circuits. Experimental results demonstrate that our circuit-based LoRA algorithm achieves an average performance improvement of 2.46% over standard LoRA with similar parameter sizes. Furthermore, we explore how combining circuits from subtasks can enhance fine-tuning in compositional tasks, providing new insights into the design of such tasks and deepening the understanding of circuit dynamics and fine-tuning mechanisms.

papers.title: Shape Happens: Automatic Feature Manifold Discovery in LLMs via Supervised Multi-Dimensional Scaling
papers.research_question: How can we reliably detect feature manifolds in language models, and do these manifolds actively support reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Supervised Multi-Dimensional Scaling (SMDS), a method for hypothesis-driven manifold analysis, and shows that feature manifolds in LLMs are stable, interpretable, and actively used in reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The findings shed light on the functional role of feature manifolds, supporting a model of entity-based reasoning in which LMs encode and transform structured representations.
papers.key_findings:
Temporal entities form feature manifolds with intuitive structures (e.g., circles, lines, clusters) that are consistent across model architectures and sizes.
Feature manifolds are dynamically adjusted depending on the task and context.
Feature manifolds actively support reasoning, as perturbing them impairs performance and manifold quality correlates with accuracy.
The method extends to other domains (e.g., geography) and to multidimensional manifolds.
Models represent temporal intervals with logarithmic compression, resembling the Weber-Fechner law.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to a set of pre-defined geometric hypotheses.
The datasets are synthetic and may not fully capture the complexity of real-world temporal reasoning.
The intervention experiments, while indicative, do not establish strict causality.
future_direction: Extend SMDS to automatically discover manifold geometries.
Apply SMDS to more complex reasoning tasks.
Investigate how manifolds evolve during training.
papers.abstract: The linear representation hypothesis states that language models (LMs) encode concepts as directions in their latent space, forming organized, multidimensional manifolds. Prior efforts focus on discovering specific geometries for specific features, and thus lack generalization. We introduce Supervised Multi-Dimensional Scaling (SMDS), a model-agnostic method to automatically discover feature manifolds. We apply SMDS to temporal reasoning as a case study, finding that different features form various geometric structures such as circles, lines, and clusters. SMDS reveals many insights on these structures: they consistently reflect the properties of the concepts they represent; are stable across model families and sizes; actively support reasoning in models; and dynamically reshape in response to context changes. Together, our findings shed light on the functional role of feature manifolds, supporting a model of entity-based reasoning in which LMs encode and transform structured representations.

papers.title: Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens (CORAL): Transferrable and Calibration-Aware Inference-Time Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve both accuracy and calibration of LLMs during inference by directly steering using correctness signals from internal activations, rather than optimizing proxies?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CORAL, a lightweight inference-time steering method that uses regularized MLP probes on residual activations to improve accuracy and calibration in MCQA tasks, with demonstrated transferability across benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CORAL provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference by extracting distributed correctness signals via regularized probes.
papers.key_findings:
CORAL consistently improves accuracy and calibration across three 7B models and multiple MCQA benchmarks.
CORAL's learned steering directions transfer without retraining to four held-out benchmarks, averaging 14% accuracy and 49% ECE improvements.
Correctness signals are distributed across many neurons and require supervised aggregation; sparse methods like SAE fail to capture them.
Middle layers (17-21) contain the most useful correctness signals for steering.
Regularized probes capture distributed correctness signals that sparse methods miss.
papers.limitation:
Limited to multiple-choice question answering; generalization to free-form generation is open.
Requires labeled data to train probes, which may not be available for all domains or languages.
Adds inference latency due to activation extraction and probe prediction.
Transfer performance depends on similarity between source and target tasks; dissimilar tasks yield smaller improvements.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit persistent miscalibration, especially after instruction tuning and preference alignment. Modified training objectives can improve calibration, but retraining is expensive. Inference-time steering offers a lightweight alternative, yet most existing methods optimize proxies for correctness rather than correctness itself. We introduce CORAL (Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens), a regularized inference-time steering method that captures distributed correctness signals from model internal activations using weight-decay MLP probes. We evaluate CORAL across three 7B-parameter models and find that it consistently improves accuracy by 10\% and expected calibration error (ECE) by 50\% on average. We additionally demonstrate that these gains transfer without retraining to the complete published test sets of four held-out benchmarks (ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, Math-MC, OpenBookQA), averaging 14\% accuracy improvements and 49\% ECE improvements. Our results support the hypothesis that distributed information in model internals can be extracted using regularized probes when individual neurons are insufficient. CORAL thus provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference.

papers.title: Carrying over algorithm in transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformer models implement the carrying over algorithm for integer addition, and how are the tasks allocated to different network components?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that transformer models implement the carrying over algorithm for integer addition in a modular fashion, with specific layers handling digit addition, carry decision, and carry addition.
papers.conclusion: Transformers implement the carrying over algorithm in a modular way, and insights from small models can inform understanding of larger models and improve generalization.
papers.key_findings:
For two-layer encoder-only models, the carrying over algorithm is implemented modularly with the first layer adding digits, the second layer deciding where to carry, and the MLP adding the carried one.
The same implementation is found in three-layer and decoder-only models.
Suggestive evidence indicates similar mechanisms in large language models like Alpaca 7B, Llemma 7B, and Zephyr 7B.
Length generalization to larger digit sums can be achieved through priming or fine-tuning.
One-layer models exhibit a phase transition in attention patterns during training.
papers.limitation: The evidence for the implementation in large language models is suggestive and not conclusive.
future_direction: Exploring better prompting strategies for large language models
Studying stabilization of attention patterns for length generalization
